resources.string: A compiler is an assembly line: lexical → syntactic → semantic → intermediate code → optimization → code generation, with the symbol table following every phase.
Lucky Sam Saw Ice On Glass! (Lexical, Syntactic, Semantic, Intermediate, Optimization, Generation)
lexical
semantic
intermediate code
Saying an undeclared variable is a syntax error (it's semantic: it depends on the symbol table).
Thinking the scanner detects a mistyped keyword (`whlie` is a valid identifier).
Mixing up a phase (logical split) with a pass (one full read of the input).
Forgetting the symbol table and error handling, which cut across every phase.
What comes out of lexical analysis?
A stream of tokens
What comes out of syntax analysis?
A parse tree
Which phase does type checking?
Semantic analysis
Front end vs back end?
Front end = analysis (understands the source); back end = synthesis (generates the target code)
What kind of error is `x = (3 + 4;`?
Syntactic
What kind of error is `int x = 3 @ 4;`?
Lexical
What kind of error is using `y` without declaring it?
Semantic
Why use intermediate code?
m languages + n machines = m + n pieces, not m × n compilers
The lexeme is the actual text, the token is the class (name + attribute) and the pattern is the rule that says which lexemes belong to the token.
The token is the drawer, the lexeme is the sock, the pattern is the label.
pattern
Counting spaces and comments as tokens.
Splitting `>=` into two tokens (longest match takes `>=` whole).
Thinking `x` and `y` are different tokens (same token id, different lexemes).
Thinking `iff` is the keyword if followed by an f.
What is a lexeme?
The sequence of source characters that matches a token's pattern
What is a token?
A pair ⟨name, attribute⟩ that represents a class of lexical units
What is a pattern?
The description (usually a regex) of a token's lexemes
Longest match rule?
Pick the longest prefix that matches some pattern
`if` matches id and keyword: which wins?
The keyword (reserved, with higher priority)
Attribute of the id token?
A pointer to the entry in the symbol table
In `fi (a == b)`, does the scanner report an error?
No: fi is a valid identifier
Regular expressions describe token patterns; Thompson turns them into an NFA, and the subset construction produces a DFA that recognizes each string with one step per character.
Thompson Transforms (regex → NFA), Subsets Simplify (NFA → DFA).
regular expression
transition

Forgetting to apply the ε-closure after the move.
Getting the precedence wrong: * > concatenation > |.

Precedence of the regex operators?
r+ written with *?
r? written with |?
Regex → NFA algorithm?
Thompson's construction
NFA → DFA algorithm?
Subset construction
What is ε-closure(T)?
The states reachable from T using only ε transitions
Maximum number of DFA states from an NFA with n states?
States of the minimal DFA for (a|b)*abb?
Can a regex recognize aⁿbⁿ?
No: the language isn't regular
A context-free grammar (N, T, P, S) generates sentences by replacing nonterminals with the right sides of productions; the parse tree sums up those replacements.
G = (N, T, P, S): Never Take a Paper unStudied.
production

In a leftmost derivation, replacing a nonterminal that isn't the leftmost one.
Thinking the derivations ⇒lm and ⇒rm generate different trees.
Mixing up a sentential form (can have nonterminals) with a sentence (terminals only).
Thinking ε can't be a leaf of the tree.
The 4 components of a CFG?
Nonterminals, terminals, productions, start symbol
What is a sentential form?
Any α such that S ⇒* α
What is a sentence?
A sentential form with terminals only
Leftmost derivation?
Always replaces the leftmost nonterminal
How many ⇒lm derivations does a tree have?
Tree leaves read from left to right?
The yield of the tree: the sentence
Language of S → a S b | ε?
Why 'context-free'?
The left side is a single nonterminal, replaced without looking at what's around it
A grammar is ambiguous if some sentence has two parse trees (two leftmost derivations); it's fixed with precedence levels or disambiguation rules.
Ambi = two: two trees for the same sentence. More precedence = deeper in the tree.
two trees

When some sentence has more than one parse tree

Deeper (far from the root)

The nearest if without an else

No, it's undecidable

The Compiler Snack Bar
Friday night, Joe's Snack Bar is packed. You write on a slip of paper: 'Deluxe burger no onions + orange juice'. That paper is your **source code**.
Wait… what does a snack bar have to do with a compiler?
Everything! The order goes through an assembly line: each person does ONE task and passes it on. A compiler is exactly that: a sequence of **phases**.
The snack bar's assembly line
The cashier reads the paper letter by letter and separates the items: [Deluxe burger] [no onions] [+] [orange juice] → **lexical analysis** (characters become tokens).
The boss checks the order is well put together: 'Deluxe with with fries no' isn't an order → **syntax analysis** (tokens become a tree).
The manager checks the MEANING: 'bean stew juice' has the shape of an order, but it doesn't exist → **semantic analysis** (types, declarations).
The order becomes a standard ticket any cook understands → **intermediate code generation**.
The kitchen notices it can toast both buns on the same grill → **optimization**.
The sandwich comes out ready → **code generation** (machine code).
What if someone on the line makes a mistake?

Each phase catches one kind of error. Unreadable writing is the cashier's job (lexical). An order that makes no sense in shape is the boss's (syntactic). An order with no meaning is the manager's (semantic).
The customer wrote 'Deluxe burger §§ fries'. Who complains FIRST?
The cashier (lexical)
The boss (syntactic)
The manager (semantic)
The cook (code generation)
'§§' isn't even a symbol on the menu: the cashier can't turn it into an item. In C, a stray character like '@' is a **lexical** error: nobody after the cashier even gets to see the problem.
And the little notebook where the cashier writes each customer's name and what they ordered? Everyone in the snack bar checks that notebook…
Who is the 'little notebook' every phase checks?
The **symbol table**: it keeps the program's names (variables, functions) with type, scope and other information. Every phase reads and writes it.

Cashier, boss and manager UNDERSTAND the order: they're the **analysis** (front end). The kitchen BUILDS the food: that's the **synthesis** (back end). The standard ticket is the bridge; swap the kitchen (another machine) and the dining room stays the same.

Q: Do the phases run one after the other, each one whole? A: In practice several phases are grouped into the same 'pass'; the parser asks the scanner 'give me the next token' on demand. But thinking of separate phases is the right way to UNDERSTAND it.
Without looking: the six phases, in order.
Lexical → Syntactic → Semantic → Intermediate code → Optimization → Code generation. And the symbol table following everyone.
Watch a program cross the conveyor
Today you'll SEE the phases working. Tap each station on the conveyor.
Tap each phase: what goes in and what comes out?
Notice: the input is a **sequence of characters** and the output is **machine code**. In between, each phase changes the program's *representation*.
My turn! I take characters and return tokens. Look at the katana:
Each color is a token class. The spaces vanish!
31 (one per character)
8: position, =, initial, +, rate, *, 60 and ;. Spaces don't become tokens; the scanner drops them.
And after the tokens, what happens?
The parser builds the tree, and the semantic phase hangs information on it, like the TYPE of each piece.
a is int, x is float. See where the semantic phase inserts type conversions.
Finding out that int mixed with float needs a conversion (inttofloat) is the job of **semantic analysis**, not syntax analysis. The tree already existed; the semantic phase only annotated it.
Three-address code: at most one operator per instruction.
Notice the order: `b * c` is computed BEFORE the sum. The parse tree decided that; the precedence was already recorded in it.
Why is it called 'THREE-address code'?
Each instruction has at most three operands: two inputs and one result, like `t1 = b * c`.
Clang is a front end (C/C++ → LLVM IR) and LLVM is the back end that optimizes and generates code for x86, ARM… The app on your phone went through a conveyor just like this.
position = initial + rate * 60, phase by phase
Let's slowly solve the most famous example from the Dragon Book. Input: `position = initial + rate * 60`, with the variables declared as float.
Solved, phase by phase
1. **Lexical**: ⟨id,1⟩ ⟨=⟩ ⟨id,2⟩ ⟨+⟩ ⟨id,3⟩ ⟨*⟩ ⟨60⟩. The number in ⟨id,1⟩ points to the row for `position` in the symbol table.
2. **Syntactic**: a tree with `=` at the root; on the right, `+`; inside the `+`, the `*`: lower down, because it has higher precedence.
3. **Semantic**: `rate` is float and `60` is an integer → it inserts the node `inttofloat(60)`.
4. **Intermediate code**: t1 = inttofloat(60); t2 = id3 * t1; t3 = id2 + t2; id1 = t3.
5. **Optimization**: converts 60 to 60.0 at compile time and removes temporaries: t1 = id3 * 60.0; id1 = id2 + t1.
6. **Code generation**: LDF R2, id3 / MULF R2, R2, #60.0 / LDF R1, id2 / ADDF R1, R1, R2 / STF id1, R1.
Intermediate code before optimizing
How did optimization make the inttofloat vanish?
Because 60 is a constant! The compiler converts it ONCE, at compile time, instead of converting it every time the program runs.
In the symbol table, position = 1, initial = 2, rate = 3. That's why `id1`, `id2`, `id3`: it's just the order in which the names appeared.
Now it's your turn, with a **faded** example: I start, you finish. Input: `total = preco * 2` (preco = price), with total and preco of type int.
**Lexical**: ⟨id,1⟩ ⟨=⟩ ⟨id,2⟩ ⟨*⟩ ⟨2⟩. **Syntactic**: `=` at the root, `*` on the right with children preco and 2.
**Semantic**: does it need any conversion?
No! preco is int and 2 is int: int * int = int. No inttofloat. (If preco were float, then yes: inttofloat(2).)
**Intermediate code** (three addresses)?
**Optimization**: can it be improved?
Yes: remove the temporary → id1 = id2 * 2. A clever optimizer could also swap `* 2` for a left shift (strength reduction).
Check with the engine (a in place of preco).
Classic question: 'show the output of each phase for assignment X'. Practice with position = initial + rate * 60 until you can do it with your eyes closed.
Why so many phases?
Today I won't explain. I'll just ask, and you'll figure it out. Guessing wrong is part of it.
Lexical analysis
Syntax analysis
Nobody: it compiles normally
'@' doesn't belong to any token pattern of the language. The scanner gets stuck before any other phase sees the code.
All the tokens are valid: x, =, (, 3, +, 4, ;. The problem is the STRUCTURE: a parenthesis opened and never closed. Structure is the syntactic phase's job.
Tokens OK, structure OK (it's a perfect assignment!). But storing a string in an int makes no SENSE. Types = semantics.
The structure is a perfect assignment. Knowing whether `y` was declared requires checking the symbol table → semantics.
Hmm… each phase catches one kind of error. So it's just splitting the work?
Right! Now another question. Imagine 5 languages and 4 different processors.
If each compiler went 'straight' from language to machine, how many would you write? And with intermediate code in the middle?
Straight: 5 × 4 = 20 compilers. With intermediate code: 5 front ends + 4 back ends = 9 pieces. That's why the front end / back end split exists!
What if you type `whlie (x)` instead of `while (x)`? Does the scanner complain?
Think: does `whlie` match the identifier pattern?
It does! Letters followed by letters is a valid identifier. The scanner happily accepts it; the error only shows up later, and `whlie (x)` even looks like a function call.
Notice? You just figured it out on your own: the scanner sees **words**, the parser sees **structure**, the semantic phase sees **meaning**.
Sum up each analysis phase as a question.
Lexical: do the characters form valid words? Syntactic: do the words form well-structured sentences? Semantic: do the sentences make sense (types, declarations)?
Compiler and phases: exam definitions

**Definition.** A *compiler* is a program that reads a program written in one language (the **source** language) and translates it into an equivalent program in another language (the **target** language), reporting the errors detected in the source program.
An *interpreter*, instead of producing a target program, directly executes the operations specified in the source program on the inputs supplied by the user.

The compiler has two parts. **Analysis** (front end): breaks the source into pieces, imposes a grammatical structure, detects errors and builds the intermediate representation and the symbol table. **Synthesis** (back end): builds the target program from the intermediate representation and the symbol table.

character stream
 → Lexical analyzer ............. token stream
 → Syntax analyzer .............. syntax tree
 → Semantic analyzer ............ syntax tree (annotated)
 → Intermediate code generator .. intermediate representation
 → Machine-indep. optimizer ..... intermediate representation
 → Code generator ............... target machine code
 → Machine-dep. optimizer ....... target machine code
Symbol table: shared by all phases
Phases of a compiler (Aho, Lam, Sethi, Ullman, ch. 1)
What each phase does (exam format)
**Lexical analysis** (scanning): reads the characters and groups them into lexemes; for each lexeme it produces a token ⟨token-name, attribute-value⟩.
**Syntax analysis** (parsing): uses the tokens to build the syntax tree, which represents the grammatical structure.
**Semantic analysis**: uses the tree and the symbol table to check consistency with the language definition; central task: type checking (including coercions).
**Intermediate code generation**: produces a low-level representation, easy to generate and to translate to the target machine (e.g. three-address code).
**Code optimization**: improves the intermediate code (faster, smaller, less energy) while preserving its meaning.
**Code generation**: maps the intermediate representation to the target language, choosing registers and instructions.
Q: Is a phase the same as a pass? A: No. A phase is a LOGICAL split of the work; a pass is one full read of the input. Several phases can be grouped into a single pass.
Which phase receives a token stream as input?
The scanner PRODUCES tokens; the parser CONSUMES them to build the tree.
Type checking is the job of which phase?
Types are about meaning: semantic analysis checks the tree and the symbol table to verify them and insert coercions.
In an essay question, write for each phase the trio **input → what it does → output**. And mention the symbol table and error handling, which cut across every phase.
Difference between compiler and interpreter, in one line.

The compiler translates the whole program into a target program (which then runs); the interpreter runs the source directly. Compiled code is usually faster; the interpreter usually gives better error diagnostics.
Lucky Sam Saw Ice On Glass!
Memorize six phases in order? Easy, if you give your brain a little push.
**L**ucky **S**am **S**aw **I**ce **O**n **G**lass! → **L**exical, **S**yntactic, **S**emantic, **I**ntermediate code, **O**ptimization, **G**eneration of code.
Picture Sam slipping on the ice. The last word is 'Glass': the last phase, code generation, where the program finally comes out.

**Memory palace**: the Compilândia map IS the pipeline. You board at the Port (source code), cut tokens in the Lexical Forest, cross the Grammar Valley and the syntax analysis fortresses, reach the Semantic City and finish at the Code Forge.
Close your eyes and walk the map: which regions, in order?
Growing zoom: **letter → word → sentence → meaning**. The scanner joins letters into words; the parser joins words into sentences; the semantic phase asks whether the sentence makes sense.
Chomsky's famous sentence: *'Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.'* Valid words ✓ (scanner OK), well-built sentence ✓ (syntax OK), zero meaning ✗ (semantics would complain!).
'The cat drank the.': at what level is the problem?
Word (lexical)
Structure (syntax)
Meaning (semantics)
All the words exist, but the sentence ends in the middle: the object is missing. A structure problem = syntactic.
Classic mix-up: 'undeclared variable' is NOT a syntax error. `y = 5;` has perfect structure; only the symbol table knows `y` doesn't exist → semantic error.
**The front end understands, the back end builds.** Front = facing the programmer (the source language); back = way behind, close to the machine.
Recite the mnemonic tapping each station.
Recite the mnemonic and say what COMES OUT of each phase.
Lexical → tokens; Syntactic → tree; Semantic → annotated tree; Intermediate → three-address code; Optimization → improved intermediate code; Generation → machine code.
The supermarket checkout
Supermarket on sale day. Lexi is at the checkout, passing the products on the belt one by one.
Beep! 'Soda 2L'. Beep! 'French bread'. Beep! 'Soda can'. For me, each product goes into a CATEGORY on the receipt.
Notice three different things: the actual product in her hand, the category printed on the receipt and the rule that says which product goes in which category.
The actual product ('Soda 2L') → **lexeme**: the real piece of text in the program, like `counter` or `42`.
The category on the receipt (DRINK) → **token**: the name of the class, like `id` or `num`.
The rule ('every bottled liquid is a DRINK') → **pattern**: the description of which lexemes belong to the token, like 'a letter followed by letters or digits'.
So 'Soda 2L' and 'Soda can' are different lexemes of the SAME token?
Exactly! Like `x` and `total`: different lexemes, same token `id`.
But on the receipt the category alone isn't enough: you need to know WHICH drink it was. That's why the token carries an **attribute**: ⟨id, pointer to `total` in the symbol table⟩.
In `if (x >= 10)`, what is the LEXEME of the comparison token?
relop (relational operator)
`>=` is the real text (lexeme). 'relop' is the token's name, the category.
And there's more: I always take the BIGGEST possible piece. Seeing `>=`, I don't cut it into `>` and `=`. It's like reading 'sunflower' as one word, not 'sun' + 'flower'.

Q: And `if`? It also matches 'letters followed by letters', the identifier pattern! A: A tie. Keywords are **reserved**: their rule has priority. But `iff` is longer than `if`, so by longest match it becomes an identifier.
Notice: `iff` and `whilex` are identifiers, not keywords!
That's why in C you can't name a variable `while`, but you can name it `whilex`.
In the analogy, who's the lexeme, who's the token and who's the pattern?
Lexeme = the actual product (the text). Token = the category on the receipt (the class). Pattern = the rule that decides the category.
Slicing code into colors
Look at my katana in action. Each color is a different token.
Tap each token to see the lexeme and the class.
Notice three things: (1) the spaces vanish; (2) `<=` is ONE token; (3) `i++` becomes two tokens, `i` and `++`.
x, +=, y and ;: 4 tokens. Even without spaces, longest match takes `+=` whole.
Without spaces, the scanner still knows where to cut.
But how does Lexi KNOW `n1` is an identifier? She follows a pattern, and a pattern is drawn as an automaton.
Identifier pattern (l = letter, d = digit). Try 'ld', 'll' and 'dl'.
'dl' was rejected! Makes sense: an identifier doesn't start with a digit.
Number pattern (d = digit, p = point). Try 'dpd', 'd' and 'dp'.
On 'dp' (like `3.`) the automaton ends on a NON-final state. So the longest valid match is just `3`; the point is left for the next token.
Check the greedy bite.
Why does the id token carry a pointer to the symbol table?
The parser only needs to know it's an `id`, but the later phases need to know WHICH one: name, type, scope. The attribute points to that entry.
Building the token table
Let's build the lexeme / token / attribute table for one line, slowly.
`if` → keyword **if**. It also matches id, but a reserved word wins. No attribute.
`(` → delimiter **(**.
`x` → **id**, attribute: pointer to x in the symbol table.
`>=` → **relop**, attribute GE. Longest match: it's not `>` + `=`.
`10` → **num**, attribute: the value 10.
`)` → delimiter **)**.
`total` → **id**, pointer to total.
`+=` → compound assignment operator **+=**.
`x` → **id**, the SAME pointer as the first x.
Check with Lexi.
The two `x`'s produce two TOKENS, but the symbol table has only ONE entry for x. Tokens repeat; table entries don't.
How many tokens?
What's the token for `while`? And for `n1`?
`while` is a keyword (reserved). `n1` is an id: it starts with a letter and then comes a digit.
Are `<=` and `++` one token each or two?
One each: longest match. `<=` is relop (LE); `++` is the increment operator.

Common question: 'how many tokens are in this snippet?'. Traps: two-character operators (`<=`, `==`, `++`), numbers with a point (`3.14` is ONE token), strings (`"a b c"` is ONE token) and comments (zero tokens).
Why is there a scanner?
I'll ask you questions. Guess without fear: getting it wrong here is part of the method.
The scanner drops spaces and comments. Why?
Because they don't change the program's meaning (in most languages)
Because they take up too much memory
Because the parser is lazy
Because spaces are forbidden in C
A space only separates lexemes; after that it's useless. (Python is the famous exception: indentation becomes INDENT/DEDENT tokens!)
In `count2=count2+1`, what is `count2`?
Two tokens: id `count` and num `2`
A single id token
A keyword
The id pattern is a letter followed by letters OR digits, and longest match swallows the 2 along with it.
How many tokens should `>=` become?
Just one. The **longest match** rule (maximal munch): take the longest prefix of the input that matches some pattern.
But what about `if`? It matches the identifier pattern AND the keyword pattern. A tie!
How do you break the tie for `if`? And why isn't `iff` a keyword?
A tie of the SAME length: the rule listed first wins, and keywords come before id. `iff` has 3 letters: longest match prefers the 3-letter id over the 2-letter `if`.
In `fi (a == f(x))`, does the scanner notice that `fi` should be `if`?
Yes, it's a lexical error
No: `fi` is a valid identifier
The scanner doesn't see context: `fi` matches the id pattern. A literal example from the Dragon Book!
Last one: why not let the parser do everything, reading character by character?
Three reasons to separate lexical from syntax analysis.

1) **Simplicity**: the grammar doesn't need to talk about spaces and comments. 2) **Efficiency**: specialized techniques (buffers, automata) read characters very fast. 3) **Portability**: the quirks of the input stay isolated in the scanner.
Scanner: 'I work with characters; you work with tokens.' Parser: 'And I call you when I need you: getNextToken()!' In practice the scanner is a subroutine of the parser.
Look: `fi` goes through as an identifier with no complaint.
Token, pattern and lexeme: definitions
**Token**: a pair ⟨token-name, attribute-value⟩. The name is an abstract symbol that represents a kind of lexical unit (keyword, identifier…); it's what the parser processes.
**Pattern**: a description of the form a token's lexemes can take. For a keyword, it's the character sequence itself; for identifiers, it's a structure matched by many strings.
**Lexeme**: a sequence of characters in the source program that matches a token's pattern and is identified by the scanner as an instance of that token.

TOKEN PATTERN (informal) LEXEMES
if characters i, f if
else characters e, l, s, e else
comparison < or > or <= or >= or == or != <=, !=
id letter followed by letters, digits pi, score, D2
number any numeric constant 3.14159, 0, 6.02e23
literal anything between quotes "core dumped"
Token examples (Dragon Book, Fig. 3.2)
Example: `E = M * C ** 2` produces ⟨id, ptr E⟩ ⟨assign_op⟩ ⟨id, ptr M⟩ ⟨mult_op⟩ ⟨id, ptr C⟩ ⟨exp_op⟩ ⟨number, 2⟩.
Skeleton of a scanner
Q: And when no pattern matches? A: **Panic mode** recovery: delete characters until a valid token is found. Other possible actions: insert, delete or replace a character, or swap two adjacent ones.
x, =, 3.14 and ;: the number with a point is a single lexeme.

Don't swap the definitions! Token = CLASS (name + attribute). Lexeme = INSTANCE (the text). Pattern = RULE (usually a regular expression). A perfect exam sentence: 'the lexeme `3.14` matches the number pattern and is reported as the token ⟨number, 3.14⟩'.
Why does the id token need an attribute and the `if` token doesn't?
Because there are infinitely many possible lexemes for id; the parser wouldn't know WHICH name it was. For `if` there's a single lexeme, so the token's name says it all.
Drawer, sock and label
**The token is the drawer**, **the lexeme is the sock** you put away, **the pattern is the label** that says which socks go in that drawer.
Another trick: **LEXeme = LEtter EXact**. It's the literal text, exactly as it appears in the code.
From abstract to concrete: **T**ype (token) → **P**rescription (pattern) → **L**iteral (lexeme).
**Memory palace**: the Lexical Forest, first stop after the Port. Lexi cuts the logs of text with her katana; each cut log is a lexeme, and she tosses each log into the right cart (the token).
**Longest match = greedy**: Lexi always bites the biggest piece she can. `>=` whole, `count2` whole, `iff` whole.
**Reserved is VIP**: on a length tie, the keyword cuts the line ahead of the identifier.
Reading `y = 42;`, what is the LEXEME of the token ⟨num, 42⟩?
The lexeme is the text `42`. 'num' is the token's name; the whole pair is the token.

Classic mix-ups: (1) thinking `x` and `y` are different tokens: same token id, different lexemes; (2) thinking the scanner catches a keyword typo (`whlie` is a valid id!); (3) counting spaces as tokens.
Fill in: 'The lexeme ___ matches the pattern ___ and becomes the token ___.'
Example: 'The lexeme `total` matches the pattern `letter(letter|digit)*` and becomes the token ⟨id, pointer to total⟩.'
Drawer, sock, label: identify each one.
The train that reads words
A little train runs through the Lexical Forest. It only moves along the tracks painted with the letter it's reading.
Each station is a **state**. Each track has a letter: it's a **transition**. Some stations have a finish flag: they're the **final** (accepting) **states**.
And how does the train decide whether the word is accepted?
It leaves the start station and reads the word letter by letter, following the tracks. The word ended at a station with a flag? Accepted! Ran out of track, or stopped far from the flag? Rejected.
The Dragon Book train: accepts words of a's and b's that end in abb. Try 'aabb' and 'abab'.
This train is a **DFA** (deterministic finite automaton): at each station, for each letter, there's AT MOST one track. The driver is never in doubt.
And what if there were two tracks with the same letter?
Then it's an **NFA** (nondeterministic): a magic train that splits and follows ALL the paths at once, like in a multiverse. And it also has ε tracks, which it takes without reading any letter.
NFA: 'I'm easy to build from the regular expression!' DFA: 'But I'm fast: one step per letter, no doubt at all.' Both recognize exactly the same languages: the regular ones.
The train factory
**Regular expression**: the drawing of the route, like `(a|b)*abb`.
**Thompson's construction**: turns the regex into an NFA, piece by piece (union, concatenation, closure).
**Subset construction**: each DFA station is a BASKET of NFA stations where the magic train could be.
**Minimization**: merges stations that behave the same. The DFA for `(a|b)*abb` ends up with 4 states.
An NFA with 3 states becomes a DFA with AT MOST how many states?
Each DFA state is a SUBSET of the NFA's states: 2³ = 8 possible subsets. In practice, it's almost always far fewer.
Lex/Flex do exactly that: you write the token regexes and they generate the DFA that becomes the heart of the scanner.
In the analogy, what are the station, track, flag and magic train?
State, transition, final (accepting) state and NFA (which can be in several states at once).
Playing with automata
Each widget is a MINIMAL DFA generated by the engine from the regular expression. Try strings and watch the path light up.
ab*: an a and then as many b's as you like. Try 'a', 'abbb' and 'ba'.
Notice: the `*` (Kleene closure) became a **loop**: a track that leaves and comes back to the same state.
Ends in abb.
In `(a|b)*abb`, after reading 'ab', what situation is the automaton in?
It already accepted
It already saw 'ab': one b is missing
It rejected forever
It went back to the start
Each state of the minimal DFA 'remembers' how much of the suffix abb it has seen: nothing, 'a', 'ab' or 'abb'. That's why there are 4 states.
Even number of a's: two states that alternate, like a light switch.
Can you make one that accepts a's and b's in the same amount, like aaabbb?
You can't! A finite automaton has finite memory: it can't count up to an arbitrary number. aⁿbⁿ needs a context-free grammar; you'll see that in the Grammar Valley.
Binary numbers with no leading zero: try '0', '101' and '011'.
Why is '011' rejected?
After reading '0', the automaton is in a final state WITH NO exits: '0' alone is accepted, but nothing can follow it. Reading '1' falls into the dead state.
The engine draws the minimal DFA WITHOUT the dead state. A transition that doesn't show up = goes to the dead state (rejection).
Now you test it: which strings are accepted?

Let's convert an NFA into a DFA, slowly. This NFA accepts the strings of a's and b's that end in ab.
NFA: at 0, reading a, the train can stay at 0 OR go to 1 (nondeterminism!)
Rule of the game: each DFA state is a **set** of NFA states, and Dtran[T, x] = ε-closure(move(T, x)). This NFA has no ε transitions, so the ε-closure adds nothing.
Start: A = ε-closure({0}) = {0}.
A on b: move({0}, b) = {0} → it's **A** itself.
Finals: the sets that contain state 2 → only **C**. Done: a DFA with 3 states.
DFA transition table (→ start, * final)
The engine reaches the same 3-state DFA. Compare!
Now faded: an NFA for strings that end in **bb**: 0 --a,b--> 0, 0 --b--> 1, 1 --b--> 2 (final).
C = {0, 1, 2}: on a? on b? Which one is final?
C on a: {0} = A. C on b: {0, 1, 2} = C. Final: C (it contains 2). A DFA with 3 states.
Check it: the engine also gives 3 states.
On the exam, organize it as a table: 'DFA state', 'NFA set' and one column per symbol. And ALWAYS apply the ε-closure after the move when the NFA has ε transitions; Thompson's has lots of them!
Discovering regular expressions
I'll show you automata and ask questions. You'll discover the rules.
Which strings does `a(a|b)*b` accept?
The ones that start with a and end with b
Only 'ab'
Any string of a's and b's
The ones that start with b
A required a, any middle of a's and b's, and a required b at the end.
Try: 'ab', 'aab', 'abba', 'ba'.
Does `x(y|z)+` accept the string 'x'?
`+` means 'one or more times': r+ = r r*. Without at least one y or z, it rejects.
Which regex describes odd binary numbers (ending in 1)?
Anything, as long as the last digit is 1. `1(0|1)*` describes the ones that START with 1.
Write `r?` using only |, concatenation and *.
`r?` = `r | ε` (zero or one time). And `r+` = `r r*`. In other words: `?` and `+` are just syntactic sugar!
Can you write a regex for balanced parentheses, like (()) and ()()?
Yes, with lots of *
No: a finite automaton can't count arbitrary depth
To know how many ')' are missing, you'd need unlimited memory. That's a job for a context-free grammar.
Now the golden question: why does the scanner use regexes and automata, and not a grammar?
Why regex/DFA in the scanner?

Tokens have a simple (regular) structure, and a DFA recognizes them in linear time: one step per character, with no backtracking. Nested structures (parentheses, blocks) are left for the parser, with grammars.
If NFA and DFA have the same power, why use an NFA?
Because an NFA is much easier to build from a regex (Thompson, piece by piece). Then we convert it to a DFA, which is fast to run.
Regex, NFA and DFA: definitions and algorithms
**Regular expression** over the alphabet Σ: ε and each a ∈ Σ are regexes; if r and s are regexes, then r|s, rs, r* and (r) are too. L(r|s) = L(r) ∪ L(s); L(rs) = L(r)L(s); L(r*) = (L(r))*.
Precedence: `*` (highest) > concatenation > `|` (lowest), all left associative. So `a|b*c` = `a|((b*)c)`.

**NFA**: (S, Σ, move, s₀, F): a finite set of states S, an alphabet Σ, a transition function that takes (state, symbol or ε) to a SET of states, a start state s₀ and final states F. **DFA**: a special case with no ε transitions and exactly one destination for each (state, symbol) pair.

Thompson's construction (regex → NFA):
 ε : i --ε--> f
 a : i --a--> f
 s|t : new i --ε--> N(s) and N(t); finals of both --ε--> new f
 st : the final of N(s) merges with the start of N(t)
 s* : i --ε--> N(s), i --ε--> f;
 final of N(s) --ε--> start of N(s) and --ε--> f
Property: N(r) has at most 2 × (number of symbols and operators in r) states.
Algorithm 3.23 (Dragon Book)
Algorithm 3.20 (Dragon Book)
**ε-closure(T)**: states reachable from some state in T using only ε transitions (includes T itself). **move(T, a)**: states reachable from T with ONE transition labeled a.
What's the correct operator precedence?
| > concatenation > *
concatenation > * > |
Like in arithmetic: * is the 'power', concatenation the 'multiplication' and | the 'sum'.
By precedence, `ab*` means…
The * applies only to the symbol right to its left: an a followed by zero or more b's.
Confirm: 'abab' is rejected.

It shows up a lot: (1) draw Thompson's NFA for `(a|b)*abb` (11 states, 0 to 10); (2) apply subsets and get A, B, C, D, E, with E final; (3) minimize by merging A and C → 4 states. Know that ε-closure({0}) = {0, 1, 2, 4, 7}.
An NFA with n states can become a DFA with up to 2ⁿ states (exponential blowup), but that's rare in practice. In exchange, simulating the DFA takes only one step per character.
Define ε-closure and move in one line each.
ε-closure(T): states reachable from T using only ε transitions (including T). move(T, a): states reachable from T by exactly one transition labeled a.

**T**hompson **T**ransforms (regex → NFA). **S**ubsets **S**implify the chaos (NFA → DFA). And **M**inimization **M**erges the repeated states.

Same precedence as in math: `*` is a power, concatenation is multiplication, `|` is a sum. Like 2 + 3·4², `a|bc*` = `a|(b(c*))`.
`*` = zero or more (the star is generous: it even accepts nothing). `+` = one or more (PLUS = at least one). `?` = maybe (zero or one).

Only the star on the 'outside' allows zero repetitions of everything. The others require at least one symbol.
The start state is already final: the empty string is accepted!

**Memory palace**: still in the Lexical Forest, the **Automaton Train**. Lexi draws the route (regex), Thompson's elves scatter ε tracks everywhere (NFA), and the driver gathers stations into baskets (subsets) so she's never in doubt (DFA).

**Regular doesn't count and doesn't nest.** Need to count or match parentheses? That's a grammar's job.

Each line is a **production**: 'a Sentence (Frase) is a noun phrase (SN) followed by a verb phrase (SV)'. Whatever appears to the left of the arrow is a **nonterminal** (a category). The real words, o, gato, come, are **terminals**.
Watch the sentence 'o gato come o peixe' (the cat eats the fish) be born, always replacing the leftmost nonterminal.
Each step replaces ONE nonterminal with the right side of one of its productions. That's a **derivation**. When we always replace the leftmost one, it's a **leftmost derivation**.
Does this grammar generate 'a menina ama o gato' (the girl loves the cat)?
Frase ⇒ SN SV ⇒ Art Sub SV ⇒ a Sub SV ⇒ a menina SV ⇒ a menina Ver SN ⇒ … ⇒ a menina ama o gato. (It doesn't care about gender agreement: 'a gato' comes out too. A toy grammar!)

Q: Why 'context-free'? A: Because the left side is ONE nonterminal alone: you can replace SN with 'Art Sub' anywhere, no matter what's around it (the context).
Regular expression: 'I describe words.' Grammar: 'I describe sentences, and I know how to nest things, like parentheses inside parentheses, something you can't do!'
In this grammar, which are the terminals and which are the nonterminals?
Nonterminals: Frase, SN, SV, Art, Sub, Ver. Terminals: o, a, gato, menina, peixe, come, ama. Start symbol: Frase (the one on the first line).

Let's watch the Dragon Book's expression grammar generate `id + id * id`.
E = expression, T = term, F = factor
Move step by step and watch the tree grow with each replacement.
On each line, the replaced nonterminal is the LEFTMOST one. The intermediate forms, like `id + T * F`, are called **sentential forms**. The last one, with terminals only, is a **sentence**.
In the leftmost derivation, after `id + T`, what's the next step?
We still need to generate `id * id` after the +. If T became F directly, the `*` would never show up! So T → T * F.
And the tree? Is it the same thing as the derivation?
The tree is the 'summary' of the derivation: it shows WHICH production was used at each node, but it forgets the ORDER of the replacements.
Read the leaves from left to right: you get the sentence.
How many steps did the derivation of `a a a b b b` take? Why?
4 steps: three times S → a S b and once S → ε. Each a gets its matching b.
Balanced parentheses. Notice how ε makes S vanish.
Difference between a sentential form and a sentence?
Sentential form: anything derivable from the start symbol (it can have nonterminals). Sentence: a sentential form with terminals only.

Question 1: try it without fear.

Every time S becomes a S b, one a AND one b come in. The number of a's and b's is always equal.

{ aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0 }: n a's followed by n b's.

Yes: a*b*
a*b* accepts aab, with different counts. No regex can do it: it would need unlimited memory. Context-free grammars describe more languages.

How many nonterminals does this grammar have?
E, T and F: the ones that appear on the left side.

Why do we need to choose WHICH nonterminal to replace in a derivation?

Because a sentential form can have several nonterminals. Fixing an order (always the leftmost, or always the rightmost) makes the derivation unique for each tree. LL parsers build the leftmost one; LR parsers, the rightmost one in reverse.
Derive it yourself before moving on.
CFGs and derivations: formal definition

**Context-free grammar** G = (N, T, P, S): N, a set of nonterminals (syntactic variables); T, a set of terminals (the tokens); P, a set of productions A → α, with A ∈ N and α ∈ (N ∪ T)*; S ∈ N, the start symbol.
**One-step derivation**: if A → γ ∈ P, then αAβ ⇒ αγβ. ⇒* means 'zero or more steps'; ⇒⁺, 'one or more steps'.
If S ⇒* α, then α is a **sentential form** of G; if α has terminals only, it's a **sentence**. The **language generated** is L(G) = { w ∈ T* | S ⇒⁺ w }.
**Leftmost derivation** (⇒lm): always replaces the leftmost nonterminal. **Rightmost** (⇒rm, or canonical): always the rightmost one.

**Parse tree**: root labeled S; internal nodes labeled with nonterminals; if a node A has children X₁…Xₙ, then A → X₁…Xₙ ∈ P; leaves are terminals or ε. The leaves read from left to right form the tree's **yield** (frontier).

Conventions (Dragon Book):
 terminals: a, b, c, +, *, (, ), id, if ...
 nonterminals: A, B, C, S, E, T, F ...
 any symbols: X, Y, Z
 strings of terminals: u, v, w, x, y, z
 sentential forms: α, β, γ
 A → α₁ | α₂ | ... | αₖ (alternatives of A)
If S ⇒* `id + T`, then `id + T` is…
a sentence
a sentential form (not a sentence)
a production
It still has the nonterminal T: it's a sentential form, but not a sentence.
Each parse tree corresponds to how many leftmost derivations?
Several
The tree fixes the productions; the 'always the leftmost' rule fixes the order. Result: a single ⇒lm derivation.
Traditional question: 'given G, show a leftmost (or rightmost) derivation of w and the tree'. A mistake that costs points: in a ⇒lm, replacing a nonterminal that is NOT the leftmost one.
Practice: the ⇒lm derivation of id * ( id + id ).
Write G = (N, T, P, S) for `S -> a S b | ε`.
N = {S}; T = {a, b}; P = {S → a S b, S → ε}; start symbol S.
The four pieces of a grammar
**G = (N, T, P, S)** → '**N**ever **T**ake a **P**aper un**S**tudied': Nonterminals, Terminals, Productions, Start symbol.
**A terminal terminates**: it's a leaf, it doesn't expand anymore. The nonterminal 'hasn't terminated' yet; it will be replaced.
Leftmost derivation = **reading a book**: you sort things out in the order you read, from left to right.

**Memory palace**: the **Grammar Valley**. Productions are seeds: a planted nonterminal (S) sprouts branches (the right side) until it's only leaves (terminals). The parse tree is, literally, a tree that grew in the valley.
A **sentential** form = a building under construction (it still has scaffolding, the nonterminals). A **sentence** = a finished building, terminals only.
In a parse tree, the terminals sit…
at the root
in the internal nodes
in the leaves
A terminal terminates: it's always a leaf. Internal nodes are nonterminals.

Classic mix-ups: (1) thinking the tree changes between ⇒lm and ⇒rm (it doesn't!); (2) mixing up derivation (from S to w) with reduction (the reverse path, used in LR); (3) forgetting that ε is a legitimate leaf.
Leaves from left to right = the sentence.
Recite: what do N, T, P, S, ⇒, ⇒* and ⇒lm mean?
Nonterminals, Terminals, Productions, Start symbol; ⇒ is one step; ⇒* is zero or more steps; ⇒lm is one step replacing the leftmost nonterminal.
The police officer and the binoculars
Newspaper headline: 'Police officer sees thief with binoculars.'
Wait: who had the binoculars? The officer or the thief?
Exactly! The sentence has TWO trees: [sees [thief with binoculars]] or [[sees thief] with binoculars]. Same words, different structure, different meaning. That's **ambiguity**.
In English, we break the tie with context. A compiler doesn't have that 'common sense': if the grammar allows two trees, it doesn't know which to pick, and each tree can mean a different program!
What's 2 + 3 * 4?
It depends on the tree
In school math, 14. But if the grammar allows the tree (2 + 3) * 4, it gives 20. The tree decides the meaning!
Short and pretty… but ambiguous
Two trees for the same sentence: an ambiguous grammar.
In the tree where * sits lower, it's computed first: 14. In the other, + sits lower: 20.
A cheap street-vendor calculator does 2 + 3 × 4 = 20 (it computes as you type). A scientific one gives 14. They're different 'grammars'!
And how do you fix it?
Two ways: rewrite the grammar with precedence levels (E, T, F) or tell the parser generator who has priority (`%left` in Bison).
E/T/F grammar: a single tree, with * lower down.
Define ambiguity in your own words.
A grammar is ambiguous if there's at least ONE sentence with two (or more) different parse trees.
Hunting twin trees
The widget looks for every tree for the input. If it finds two, it shows both.
Look at the ROOT of each tree: in one, the first production is E → E + E; in the other, E → E * E. Different roots = different structures.
And `id + id + id`, in this same grammar?
One tree
(id + id) + id or id + (id + id). With + the value is the same, but with - it isn't: (5 - 3) - 1 ≠ 5 - (3 - 1). It's an **associativity** problem.
Associativity: who joins up first?
In the E/T/F grammar, left recursion forces (id + id) + id.
And the famous 'dangling else'?
i = 'if (cond) then', e = 'else', x = any statement
Does the else belong to the first if or the second?
C, Java and friends decide: the else matches the **nearest** if that doesn't have an else yet. Yacc/Bison implements that by preferring shift in the conflict.
Why is ambiguity a problem for a compiler?
Because each tree can have a different meaning (14 or 20; the else of one if or the other). The compiler needs ONE deterministic translation.

Leftmost derivation #2 (* at the root)

Yes, one is enough
No, it has to be most of them
Only if all of them do

Both generate every expression with +, *, parentheses and id. One is ambiguous; the other isn't.

Is ambiguity a property of the grammar or of the language?

Of the GRAMMAR, in general: the same language can have ambiguous and unambiguous grammars. (There are 'inherently ambiguous' languages, where EVERY grammar is ambiguous; they're rare and don't show up in programming languages.)
In the E/T/F grammar, why does * always sit lower in the tree?
Because * only appears in T, one level below E
By luck
Because * is written first
To reach a *, you have to go through T; and T only appears below E. Each level of the grammar is a level of precedence.
And why does `id + id + id` group to the left in E → E + T?
Because the recursion is on the left: only the left E can contain another +
Because the parser reads from the left
The right operand is a T, which doesn't contain + (without parentheses). So the 'extra' + only fits in the left subtree.
Is there a program that says whether ANY grammar is ambiguous?
Is there an algorithm that decides, for any CFG, whether it's ambiguous?
No: it's an undecidable problem
Undecidable! That's why we use sufficient conditions: if the grammar is LL(1) or LR(1), it's certainly not ambiguous.
Two ways to deal with an ambiguous grammar.

1) Rewrite the grammar (precedence levels; else matching the nearest if). 2) Keep the ambiguous one and give the generator disambiguation rules (in Bison: %left, %right, %nonassoc and a preference for shift).
Ambiguity: definition and disambiguation

**Definition.** A grammar G is **ambiguous** if there's some sentence w ∈ L(G) with more than one parse tree. Equivalently: w has more than one leftmost derivation, or more than one rightmost derivation.
A language is **inherently ambiguous** if every CFG that generates it is ambiguous. Example: { aⁱbʲcᵏ | i = j or j = k }.
**Fact.** There's no algorithm that decides whether an arbitrary CFG is ambiguous (the problem is undecidable).

Disambiguating expressions (one level per precedence):
 E → E + T | T (+ : lowest precedence, left assoc.)
 T → T * F | F (* : highest precedence, left assoc.)
 F → ( E ) | id (atoms)
Rules:
 the LOWEST-precedence operator sits closest to the root;
 LEFT recursion → left associativity;
 RIGHT recursion → right associativity (e.g. ^).
Dangling else without ambiguity (Dragon Book, §4.3.2)
To prove G is ambiguous, it's enough to show…
one ⇒lm derivation and a different ⇒rm derivation for w
two different ⇒lm derivations for the same w
that G has left recursion
Two distinct ⇒lm = two distinct trees. One ⇒lm and one ⇒rm can belong to the same tree; and left recursion has nothing to do with ambiguity.
Every LL(1) or LR(1) grammar is…
unambiguous
it depends on the input
A deterministic parser builds ONE tree per input; if the table has no conflicts, the grammar isn't ambiguous.

Classic: 'Show that the if-then-else grammar is ambiguous using `if E1 then if E2 then S1 else S2`' and 'give an equivalent unambiguous grammar'. Memorize the matched/open idea: between a then and an else only a 'matched' statement can come.
The classic counterexample, in miniature.
Why does left recursion give left associativity?
In E → E + T, the operand that can contain other +'s is the LEFT one. In a + b + c, a + b becomes the left subtree: (a + b) + c.
Two trees, one problem
**Ambi = two.** An ambidextrous person uses both hands; an ambiguous grammar has TWO trees for the same sentence.
Proof of ambiguity = **'two from the same hand'**: two leftmost (or two rightmost). One from each hand doesn't count!
**Precedence = depth.** Whoever has MORE precedence sits DEEPER in the tree (it's computed first). The + sits near the root; the * further down.
**Recursion points to associativity.** E → **E** + T: left recursion → left associative. P → B ^ **P**: right recursion → right associative.
**Memory palace**: in the Grammar Valley there are two twin trees planted side by side, with the same sign: `id + id * id`. It's the **Two Trees** minigame.
**The dangling else goes with the neighbor**: the else stays with the nearest if that's still unpaired.
In `2 ^ 3 ^ 2` (power, right associative), what's the correct grouping?
Right associative: the rightmost one joins first. 3² = 9, and 2⁹ = 512.

Classic mix-ups: (1) thinking ambiguity belongs to the language; it almost always belongs to the grammar; (2) thinking left recursion causes ambiguity: E → E + T is left recursive and NOT ambiguous; (3) thinking you can always test ambiguity automatically (it's undecidable).
The twins: same sign, different structures.
Recite the hooks: ambi, same hand, depth, neighbor.
Ambiguous = two trees; prove it with two derivations from the same hand (lm with lm); higher precedence = deeper; the else goes with the neighboring if.
The dog chasing its tail
A government office. A sign on the wall: 'To get document A, show document A.'
But… that's impossible! I never get anywhere!
Well, that's exactly what happens to a **top-down** parser facing `E -> E + T`.
In recursive descent, each nonterminal becomes a function. Function E() tries the production E → E + T: 'to recognize E, first recognize E'. It calls E()… which calls E()… which calls E()…
Infinite loop → stack overflow
E()… E()… E()… E()… I… only… see… the… top… and… it… won't… stop… growing… I BURST.
The problem isn't having recursion, it's the recursion being the FIRST thing, before consuming any token. A dog chasing its tail: it spins and spins and goes nowhere.
And how do you get out of the loop?
Look at what `E -> E + T | T` really generates: a T and then as many '+ T' as you like. T + T + T… So we start with the T (the part that is NOT recursive) and leave the repetition for the end.
Same language, recursion now on the RIGHT
It's like fixing the office sign: 'Show your ID. Then, if you want, more documents.' Something concrete first; the repetition after.
Before and after: E and T got the helpers E' and T'.
Does the new grammar generate the same language?

Left factoring algorithm

**Left factoring** is a grammar transformation useful for producing grammars suitable for predictive (top-down) parsing. When the choice between two alternatives of A isn't clear, we rewrite A's productions to put off the decision until enough input has been seen.

Input: grammar G. Output: an equivalent factored grammar.
for each nonterminal A:
 find the LONGEST prefix α common to two or more alternatives
 if α ≠ ε:
 replace A → αβ₁ | αβ₂ | ... | αβₙ | γ
 with A → αA' | γ
 A' → β₁ | β₂ | ... | βₙ
 (γ = alternatives that don't start with α; A' is new)
repeat until no pair of alternatives of a nonterminal has a common prefix

FIRST step by step
1) Terminals are their own FIRST: FIRST(int) = {int}, FIRST(id) = {id}, FIRST(,) = {,}.
2) T → int | float: both productions start with a terminal. FIRST(T) = {int, float}.
3) L → id R: starts with the terminal id. FIRST(L) = {id}.
4) R → , id R | ε: the first starts with ',' and the second is ε. FIRST(R) = {',', ε}.
5) D → T L ;: starts with T, which is NOT nullable. I copy FIRST(T) and stop. FIRST(D) = {int, float}.

FIRST: definition and algorithm (exam version)
Now in a suit and tie. This is the version you write on the exam.
**Definition.** For a string α of grammar symbols, FIRST(α) = { a terminal | α ⇒* a β }. If α ⇒* ε, then ε ∈ FIRST(α) too.
Rules for each symbol X
1. If X is a terminal, FIRST(X) = {X}.
2. If X → ε is a production, add ε to FIRST(X).
3. If X → Y1 Y2 … Yk: add FIRST(Y1) − {ε}; if ε ∈ FIRST(Y1), add FIRST(Y2) − {ε}; and so on. If ε ∈ FIRST(Yi) for every i, add ε.
4. Repeat until no set changes (fixed point).
Fixed point: the sets only grow and the number of terminals is finite, so the loop ends. (With k = 0, A → ε, the ε goes in.)
**FIRST of a string** α = X1 X2 … Xn: same reasoning. Add FIRST(X1) − {ε} and move on while the current symbol is nullable; ε ∈ FIRST(α) only if all the Xi are nullable (or if α = ε).
Why does 'only grow' guarantee it ends?
Because there's a finite number of terminals. Each round that changes something adds at least one element; at some point there's nothing left to add.
In S → A B c, A → a | ε, B → b | ε, what's FIRST(A B)?
A is nullable → I look at B; B is nullable too → ε goes in. FIRST(A B) = {a, b, ε}. The c isn't part of the string A B!

FOLLOW: definition and algorithm (exam version)
Exam version, spelled out.

**Definition.** For a nonterminal A, FOLLOW(A) is the set of terminals a that can appear immediately to the right of A in some sentential form, that is, S ⇒* α A a β. If A can be the rightmost symbol of a sentential form, $ ∈ FOLLOW(A).
Rules (apply until nothing changes)
1. Put $ in FOLLOW(S), where S is the start symbol.
2. For each production A → α B β: everything in FIRST(β), except ε, goes into FOLLOW(B).
3. For each production A → α B, or A → α B β with ε ∈ FIRST(β): everything in FOLLOW(A) goes into FOLLOW(B).
Notice: FIRST(ε) = {ε}. That's why, when B is at the end (β empty), rule 3 fires.

It's rule 1. FOLLOW never contains ε, and there's no general relation between FOLLOW(A) and FIRST(A).

FOLLOW(A) = {a, b} and FOLLOW(B) = {a, b}. After the first A comes a, after the second comes b; the same for B. (Classic example: the grammar is LL(1) even with A and B nullable.)
So: $ in the start symbol, look to the right, and if it's over or can vanish, inherit from the parent.

Recursive descent: exam definition
Exam definition, Dragon Book style.
A **recursive descent parser** is a set of procedures, one for each nonterminal. Execution starts with the start symbol's procedure and succeeds if it finishes having consumed the whole input.
Typical procedure for a nonterminal A.

In the general form, choosing the production may require **backtracking**. In the **predictive** form, the lookahead decides: use A → α if look ∈ FIRST(α), or if α ⇒* ε and look ∈ FOLLOW(A). That requires an **LL(1)** grammar.
Requirements for predictive recursive descent
No left recursion (direct or indirect): otherwise, infinite loop.
Left factored: otherwise, one token doesn't decide.
LL(1) conditions satisfied: alternatives with disjoint choice sets.
If no alternative fits the lookahead: error (unless there's an ε alternative and look ∈ FOLLOW(A)).

Shift-reduce: exam definitions
Exam definitions, no fluff.
**Shift-reduce parsing**: bottom-up parsing with a stack of grammar symbols and an input buffer. Starting configuration: stack $, input w$. Success: stack $ S, input $.
The four actions
**Shift**: moves the next input symbol to the top of the stack.
**Reduce**: the top holds a right side β (the handle); pop β and push A, for A → β.
**Accept**: announces successful completion.
**Error**: detects a syntax error and calls the recovery routine.
**Handle.** If S ⇒*rm α A w ⇒rm α β w, then the production A → β at the position right after α is a handle of α β w. (w has terminals only; 'rm' = rightmost.)
**Viable prefix**: a prefix of a right sentential form that doesn't go past the end of the handle. The stack contents are always a viable prefix.
The sequence of reductions of a shift-reduce parser, read back to front, corresponds to:
An ambiguous tree
Bottom-up = rightmost derivation in reverse. It's the R in LR.
**shift/reduce**: it can't decide between shifting and reducing (e.g. the dangling else).
**reduce/reduce**: it can't decide which reduction to do.
Grammars with a conflict for a method don't belong to its class (e.g. they aren't SLR(1)). Ambiguous grammars always produce a conflict.
Follow the definitions in the parsing of ( id ).

The standard answer is the Stack | Input | Action table, with the production used in each 'reduce'. And know by heart: the handle is always on top; LR = Left-to-right, Rightmost derivation (in reverse).
Define handle in one sentence.
A substring that matches the right side of a production and whose reduction represents a step back in a rightmost derivation.

LL vs LR by the fireside. LL: 'I pick the production looking only at its first token.' LR: 'I see the WHOLE right side plus one token before deciding. I'm patient, and that's why I accept more grammars, including left-recursive ones.' LL: 'But I'm easy to write by hand!' LR: 'That's why they invented Bison for me.'
Shift until you see the handle
Gate of the Bottom-Up Fortress: a factory conveyor carries little boxes (tokens) to an assembler.
**'Shift until you see the handle; found the handle on top, reduce.'** Handle = the grip you grab to fold everything into the rule's left side.
**LR = 'Left to right, Rebuilds the rightmost… back to front.'** Bottom-up = rightmost in reverse.
**Reduce = 'take out the right side, put in the left side'.** Like trading a handful of coins for a bill.
Top-down × bottom-up
Top-down (Temple): starts at the root S and predicts. Bottom-up (Fortress): starts at the leaves and builds.
LL: leftmost derivation, in order. LR: rightmost derivation, reversed.
LL stack: what's left (future). LR stack: what's been seen (past).
Left recursion: forbidden in LL, fine in LR.
And is 'shift' pushing or moving?
Both! The token moves from the input onto the stack. In the Dragon Book's words: **shift** and **reduce**.
Which action consumes an input token?
All of them
Only shift consumes input. Reduce only touches the stack (swaps β for A).

The bookmark
Central tower of the Bottom-Up Fortress. Each floor is a 'state' full of bookmarks.
An **LR(0) item** is a production with a dot • in the middle: a bookmark of where you are in the reading. C → c • C means: 'I've seen the c, now I expect a C'.
Our recipe book. It generates strings like d d, c d d, c c d c d…
Like a download progress bar?
Right! Dot at the start (C → • c C): 0%. Dot at the end (C → c C •): 100%, time to **reduce**.
How many LR(0) items does the production S → C C produce?
Now the magic of **closure**. If I expect a C (dot before C), then I may be at the start of any recipe for C. I 'invite' C → • c C and C → • d.
Closure = **a cascade of invitations**: the nonterminal right after the dot invites its own productions, with the dot at the start. The guests invite theirs too.
And the **goto**: moving the dot over a symbol. goto(I, c) = take the items with • before c, move the dot past the c and close again.
The whole building: 7 floors (states I0 to I6) and the stairs (transitions) between them.
In state I0, which items are there? (Hint: start with S' → • S and keep inviting.)
Q: What's this S'? A: It's the **augmented grammar**: we create S' → S to have a single accepting item, S' → S •.
Bookmark, invitation, step. Items, closure, goto. I like it!
Exploring the LR(0) automaton
Explore the LR(0) automaton the way you'd explore a map.
Tap each state to see its items. The arrows are the gotos.
Exploration guide
I0 --S--> I1 = { S' → S • }: the accepting state.
I0 --C--> I2 = { S → C • C, C → • c C, C → • d }: the dot moved past the first C, and the second C invited its productions.
I0 --c--> I3 = { C → c • C, C → • c C, C → • d }. Notice I3 --c--> I3: a loop!
I0 --d--> I4 = { C → d • }: a complete item → reduction.
I5 = { S → C C • } and I6 = { C → c C • }: two more reduction states.
From I2, reading d, which state do we go to?
A new state
goto(I2, d) = { C → d • } = I4. If the set of items already exists, we reuse the state: that's why the automaton is finite.
Why does I3, reading c, go back to I3?
Because goto(I3, c) gives C → c • C again, and the closure repeats the same guests. Same set = same state. It's the automaton 'counting' the c's without needing extra memory.
Now a bigger grammar: 12 states (I0 to I11). Look for the state that has E → T • and T → T • * F together.
What problem would that state (E → T • together with T → T • * F) cause if we always reduced when an item is complete?
A shift-reduce conflict on '*': the complete item says reduce E → T and the other says shift *. Pure LR(0) can't solve it; SLR(1) uses FOLLOW(E) = {+, ), $} to decide (next room).
The LR(0) automaton recognizes exactly the grammar's **viable prefixes**. Look at the paths from I0: each path spells something that can be on the stack.

Items, CLOSURE, GOTO and the canonical collection (exam version)
Formal definitions, as in the Dragon Book.
**LR(0) item**: a production of G with a dot at some position on the right side. A → X Y Z produces A → • X Y Z, A → X • Y Z, A → X Y • Z and A → X Y Z •. The production A → ε produces only A → •.
**Augmented grammar** G': G with a new start symbol S' and the production S' → S. The parser accepts when it would reduce by S' → S.
Closure of a set of items.
Goto: move the dot over X and close.
Canonical collection of sets of LR(0) items.
**Kernel items**: S' → • S and all the items with the dot not at the left end. The others are **nonkernel** items and can be recomputed by the closure.
Which of these is a kernel item?
Identify, in each state, which items are kernel items.
Typical question: 'compute CLOSURE({…})' or 'GOTO(I, X)'. Don't forget: GOTO = move the dot **and then** close. And A → ε produces only the item A → •, which is born complete.
What's the relationship between the LR(0) automaton and the viable prefixes?
The automaton recognizes exactly the viable prefixes: γ is viable if and only if the path GOTO(I0, γ) exists from the start state.

**The dot • is the 'you are here'.** To its left: what's already on the stack (past). To its right: what's left to read (future).
**CLOSURE = 'invite the family'.** Dot before a nonterminal B? Call all of B's productions, with the dot at the start. B's family invites their own families.
**GOTO = 'goal!': kick the dot one step forward and then celebrate with the family (closure).**
The closure only adds items with the dot AT THE START (B → • γ).
The goto moves the dot only in the items with • before X; the others are left out.

The açaí bar that follows the chart
Bottom-Up Fortress, west wing. On the wall, a giant chart full of cells: s5, r2, acc, empty, empty, s7...
It looks like a spreadsheet gone wrong. What's that for?
It's the brain of an LR parser: the ACTION/GOTO table. I'll explain it with an açaí bar.

The server builds açaí cups. She **puts ingredients in the cup** one by one (shift). When the cup has a complete combination, açaí + granola + banana, she **swaps it all for a name**: 'Classic Combo' (reduce).
She doesn't think: she looks at **where she is in the order** (the state) and **the customer's next request** (the token), and obeys the chart on the wall.
Moment in the order (what's already in the cup) → **state** of the LR(0) automaton
Customer's next request → **lookahead token**
'Put it in the cup and go to moment 7' → **shift 7** (s7)
'Swap açaí+granola+banana for Classic' → **reduce** by Classic → açaí granola banana
'With a Classic in hand, go to moment 4' → **GOTO**[state, Classic] = 4
'What can come AFTER a Classic' → **FOLLOW(Classic)**
I am... the stack. I only see... my top. The chart says... the rest. I like charts.
The cup has açaí + granola + banana (a complete Classic). The next request is 'condensed milk'. Under the SLR rule, when does she close the Classic?
Always: full cup = close it right away
Only if 'condensed milk' can come AFTER a Classic (it's in FOLLOW)
Never: she only shifts
SLR only puts 'reduce' in the FOLLOW columns. If condensed milk never comes after a Classic, closing now would be a guaranteed mistake.
If the same cell of the chart says 'put it in the cup' AND 'close the combo', the server gets stuck. That's a **shift/reduce conflict**. Two different 'close' orders = **reduce/reduce**.
The real chart for E → E + T | T ...: no cell with two orders: the grammar is SLR(1).
In the analogy, what plays the role of FOLLOW?
The list of what can come right after a combo. The server only closes the combo (reduces) if the next request is on that list.

Why 'Simple'? Because SLR uses the simplest possible LR(0) automaton and decides reductions with FOLLOW, which you already know how to compute. Simple, but a bit nearsighted, and that's going to be a topic.

Four rules to fill in the table
Arrow with **terminal** a from Ii to Ij → ACTION[i, a] = **sj**
Arrow with **nonterminal** A from Ii to Ij → GOTO[i, A] = **j**
Complete item **A → α •** in Ii → **rN** in ACTION[i, a] for each a in **FOLLOW(A)**
Item **E' → E •** in Ii → ACTION[i, $] = **acc**

Reduce by E → T
Shift '*' (s7)

'*' isn't in FOLLOW(E) = { +, ), $ }, so the reduce isn't even written in that column. Only the shift is left. A fight avoided by FOLLOW!
Follow the stack: in state 9, with '*', it shifts; only later does it reduce T → T * F.
See? I kept E + T... and waited for the '*'. That's why... multiplication binds tighter.
Now a grammar where FOLLOW saves nobody.
Why did '=' get into FOLLOW(R)?
This grammar is NOT ambiguous. The conflict is SLR's fault for being nearsighted: no sentential form starts with 'R ='. Keep this one in mind: it's the gateway to LALR.

Why does FOLLOW decide the reductions?
Today I'll only ask. Answer in your head before tapping; getting it wrong here is practice, not a grade.
A state has the item A → α •. What is that dot at the end saying?
That the top of the stack holds the whole α: we have a handle candidate. We can reduce by A → α.
Pure LR(0) reduces on ANY next token. What if the same state also has B → β • a γ?
On token a, it wants to reduce AND shift: a conflict. LR(0) is blind to the future.
If we reduce to A, which tokens can show up right after in a valid derivation?
Only those in FOLLOW(A). If the next token isn't there, reducing to A is a guaranteed error.
So SLR is LR(0) with a FOLLOW filter on the reductions!
Exactly. Same automaton, same states, just more polite reductions.
And if token a is in FOLLOW(A) and the state also has B → β • a γ?
SLR picks shift on its own
Shift/reduce conflict: the grammar isn't SLR(1)
SLR reduces by the shortest rule
The SLR table doesn't pick anything: if two actions land in the same cell, the grammar simply isn't SLR(1). (The one that picks 'shift' by default is Bison, a different story.)
And two complete items A → α • and B → β • in the same state?
If FOLLOW(A) ∩ FOLLOW(B) ≠ ∅, a reduce/reduce conflict in those columns.
Does every ambiguous grammar produce a conflict in the SLR table?
Yes: no ambiguous grammar is LR(k). But the converse is false; a conflict in SLR doesn't prove ambiguity (remember S → L = R | R?).
Why is FOLLOW too coarse?
It lumps together everything that can follow A ANYWHERE in the grammar, without knowing which path you came from. Recovering that context is LR(1)'s job.
Think: how would you carry, inside each item, the information 'what can come after THIS A, on this path'? Hold on to that idea until the LALR lesson.
Building the SLR(1) table: algorithm
Let G' be the augmented grammar (S' → S) and C = { I0, ..., In } the canonical collection of sets of LR(0) items of G'. State i corresponds to Ii; the start state is closure({ [S' → • S] }).
SLR(1) algorithm (Dragon Book, Alg. 4.46)
**Definition.** G is SLR(1) if and only if no ACTION cell gets more than one action.
The two kinds of conflict
**Shift/reduce:** Ii contains [A → α • a β] and [B → γ •] with a ∈ FOLLOW(B)
**Reduce/reduce:** Ii contains [A → α •] and [B → β •] with FOLLOW(A) ∩ FOLLOW(B) ≠ ∅

push state 0; a := first token
repeat:
 s := state on top
 case ACTION[s, a]:
 shift t: push t; a := next token
 reduce A → β: pop |β| states; t := top
 push GOTO[t, A]; output A → β
 accept: stop with success
 error: call error recovery
The LR parser algorithm (the same for SLR, LALR and LR(1); only the table changes)
SLR(1) table of the expression grammar: no conflicts.
Which statement is TRUE (about grammar classes)?
Every SLR(1) grammar is LL(1)
Every SLR(1) grammar is LALR(1)
Every LALR(1) grammar is SLR(1)
Hierarchy: LR(0) ⊂ SLR(1) ⊂ LALR(1) ⊂ LR(1). LL(1) and SLR(1) are incomparable (E → E + T is SLR but not LL).
Dimensions of the table?
One row per LR(0) state. ACTION: one column per terminal + $. GOTO: one column per nonterminal (without S').
A transition on a terminal becomes a 'shift' in ACTION; a transition on a nonterminal becomes a number in GOTO. There's no 'shift' in GOTO and no plain number in ACTION.
To justify a conflict, cite: state, terminal, the two items and the FOLLOW. E.g.: 'I2, column =: s6 from S → L • = R and r5 from R → L •, since = ∈ FOLLOW(R)'.
The FOLLOW doorman of the SLR tower
Memory Palace: Bottom-Up Fortress, the SLR tower. At the door, a doorman with a clipboard named FOLLOW.
SLR = **'Sure, Let it Reduce'**, but only if the next token is on FOLLOW's clipboard.

• before a TERMINAL → sN (shift and go to N)
• at the END of the item → rN (only in the FOLLOW columns)
S' → S • → acc (only in the $ column)
arrow with a NONterminal → GOTO (plain number)
Pocket cheat sheet
Dot in front of a terminal: **'there's road, keep going'** (shift). Dot at the end: **'arrived, close it'** (reduce).
**S/R** = one item wants to move and another wants to close (one door, two commands). **R/R** = two items want to close at the same time (two names for the same package).
I cut tokens; the doorman only lets reduce whoever he knows. Teamwork!
Only lets it shift
Allows the reduction AND the arrow shows shift: an S/R conflict
Doesn't allow anything
The doorman only looks at the global clipboard (FOLLOW). He doesn't know that, there, an R is never followed by '='. Nearsighted!

LR(0): 'I reduce whenever I see a complete item, without looking at anyone!' SLR: 'And that's why you fight with everyone. I ask FOLLOW first.' LALR (from the back): 'You two will still come asking me for help...'
Recite the four rules of the SLR table.
Terminal after the dot → shift. Nonterminal → GOTO. Complete item → reduce in the FOLLOW columns. S' → S • → accept on $.
Contrast: in LL(1), FOLLOW only comes in for the productions that derive ε. In SLR, FOLLOW decides EVERY reduction.
A bus with the destination on its forehead
SLR got stuck on that pointer grammar. Just throw it away?
No! Let's give the parser some extra information. Think of a bus company.
Each **item** is a passenger on a **route** (the production with the dot). SLR drops passengers off at any stop that **some** route in the city uses: that's the global FOLLOW.
**LR(1)** sticks the **exact stop** where each passenger gets off on their forehead: the **lookahead**. LR(1) item = [route, destination], e.g. [R → L •, $].
Bus route → the item's **core** (A → α • β)
Drop-off stop on the forehead → **lookahead** (a terminal)
Getting off the bus → **reduce**, only when the next token is the lookahead
Huge fleet, one bus per route+destinations combination → **canonical LR(1)** (many states)
Merging buses with the same routes, adding up destinations → **LALR(1)**
More buses... more states... more memory. The company... complained.
So the company merges buses that run exactly the **same routes** (same core) and joins the destination lists. The fleet goes back to the size of LR(0)/SLR!
Bus 1: passenger A gets off at d, B gets off at e. Bus 2 (same routes): A gets off at e, B gets off at d. Merging the two, what happens at stop d?
Nothing, only A gets off
A and B both want to get off: chaos (reduce/reduce)
Both stay on the bus
Merged, A and B have d and e on their foreheads. At stop d, two 'reduces' fight over the cell: a reduce/reduce conflict LR(1) didn't have.
Merging never creates a new shift/reduce conflict: who 'keeps riding' (shift) depends only on the route, and the routes are the same. Only the 'get off' part (lookahead) is added up.
SLR gets stuck at [2, =]. In LR(1), state 2 has [R → L •, $]: it only gets off at $, so '=' is left with just the shift.
In the analogy, what's a state's 'core'?
The set of routes (items without the lookahead). LR(1) states with the same core become a single state in LALR.
Yacc and Bison generate LALR(1) tables by default: almost the power of LR(1) with the size of SLR. Modern Bison also offers IELR and canonical LR(1) via %define lr.type.

An LR(1) grammar that isn't LALR(1)
Bison reports 2 reduce/reduce conflicts and picks the rule that appears first (x : c).
With Bison's default choice, what happens to the valid sentence 'a c e'?
It's accepted
It gives a syntax error, even though it's valid
Bison asks the user
On 'e', it reduces c to x (first rule), but 'a x e' doesn't exist, only 'a y e'. The merge made the parser lose a sentence of the language.
Notice: LR(1) kept 'a c' and 'b c' in different states. The merge mixed the contexts; that's exactly where LALR is weaker than LR(1).
LR(1) closure and merging, step by step
Let's compute I0 of the grammar S → L = R | R; L → * R | id; R → L, with lookaheads.
Start with [S' → • S, $]
Dot before S; what comes after S is ε, so the lookahead is FIRST($) = { $ } → [S → • L = R, $] and [S → • R, $]
From [S → • R, $]: nothing comes after R → FIRST($) → [R → • L, $]
From [R → • L, $]: → [L → • * R, $] and [L → • id, $]
Nothing new? Done. Compacting: [L → • * R, =/$] and [L → • id, =/$]
The rule is FIRST(β a), where β is what comes AFTER the nonterminal in the item and a is the item's lookahead. Not FOLLOW!
Move the dot over L: [S → L • = R, $] and [R → L •, $]
Closure adds nothing (dot before a terminal or at the end)
Table: '=' → shift; R → L • reduces ONLY on $ → no conflict!
My turn! My turn!
Compute GOTO(I0, *).
[L → * • R, =/$] and, closing: [R → • L, =/$], [L → • * R, =/$], [L → • id, =/$]. The lookaheads of L → * R are inherited by R → • L because R is at the end.
In LR(1) there's [L → id •, =/$] (after 'id' at the start) and [L → id •, $] (after 'L = id'). Do they merge in LALR? Is there a conflict?
They merge (same core L → id •) into [L → id •, =/$]. A single complete item → no conflict.
In the grammar S → a A d | b B d | a B e | b A e; A → c; B → c, which LR(1) states merge and what happens?
{ [A → c •, d], [B → c •, e] } and { [B → c •, d], [A → c •, e] } have the same core. Merged: A → c • and B → c • both on d and on e → reduce/reduce.
Fun fact: SLR also has this R/R (FOLLOW(A) = FOLLOW(B) = { d, e }). Only canonical LR(1) escapes it.
Typical question: 'show that G is LR(1) but not LALR(1)'. Recipe: find two LR(1) states with the same core whose complete items swap lookaheads, merge them and point to the cell with two reduces.
What if the item knew the future?
Remember the question from the last lesson? How do you carry, inside the item, 'what comes after this A, on this path'?
What's the simplest idea?
Stick a terminal on the item: [A → α • β, a] means 'when α β is complete, only reduce if the next token is a'.
Where does the lookahead of the new items in the closure come from?
From the item that created them: in [A → α • B β, a], each B → • γ gets lookaheads FIRST(β a). It's the local context, not the global FOLLOW.
Why does that solve S → L = R | R?
In state 2, R → L • came from S → • R, $, so it only reduces on $. The '=' is left with just the shift.
What's the price?
Many states: the same core shows up repeated with different lookaheads. For real languages, canonical LR(1) can have thousands more states.
What if we merged the states that only differ in the lookahead?
You just invented LALR(1). The names you didn't know were already in your head.
Can merging states with the same core create a new SHIFT/REDUCE conflict?
No: if it showed up after, it already existed in one of the original states
Only if the grammar is ambiguous

Shifts depend only on the core. If [A → α •, a] and [B → β • a γ] are in the merged state, some original state had [A → α •, a] and, having the same core, also [B → β • a γ, ...]. The conflict was already there.
And a new reduce/reduce?
It can! Two states with no conflict, with A and B complete and swapping lookaheads (d/e and e/d), become one state with two reduces on d and on e.
So why does Bison use LALR and not LR(1)?
Because LALR has the same number of states as SLR and is almost always enough for programming languages. The rare R/R from merging is worth the savings.
SLR: 'I use FOLLOW and that's it.' LALR: 'I use real lookaheads, just merged: smarter than you and the same size.' LR(1): 'And I never merge anything. Stronger than both... and a lot bulkier.'
LR(1) items, closure and merging: definitions
**LR(1) item:** a pair [A → α • β, a] with A → α β ∈ P and a ∈ T ∪ { $ }. The first component is the **core**; a is the **lookahead**. The lookahead only has an effect when β = ε.

CLOSURE(I):
 repeat
 for each [A → α • B β, a] in I
 for each production B → γ
 for each b in FIRST(β a)
 add [B → • γ, b] to I
 until no change
 return I

GOTO(I, X) := CLOSURE({ [A → α X • β, a] | [A → α • X β, a] ∈ I })

start state := CLOSURE({ [S' → • S, $] })
Building the canonical LR(1) collection
**LR(1) table:** the same as SLR, except that [A → α •, a] generates a reduce **only** in ACTION[i, a] (not in all of FOLLOW(A)).

LALR(1):
 1. build the LR(1) collection C = { I0, ..., In }
 2. group the sets with the same core;
 replace each group with the UNION of its items
 3. build ACTION as in LR(1); if there's a conflict,
 the grammar isn't LALR(1)
 4. GOTO(J, X) := the state that contains GOTO(Ik, X)
 (well defined: same cores → same destinations)

FIRST(β a): if β doesn't derive ε, the a doesn't even show up; if it does, the parent's lookahead 'passes through'. FOLLOW(B) would be going back to SLR.

Memory Palace: the top floor of the Bottom-Up Fortress. A tailor sews identical twins into one, adding up both of their clothes.
**Same skeleton, clothes added up.** States with the same core (skeleton) become one; the lookaheads (clothes) are joined.
Glasses: **LR(0)** = no glasses. **SLR** = blurry binoculars (global FOLLOW). **LR(1)** = a magnifying glass on each item. **LALR** = a magnifying glass, but sewn in pairs.

Yacc/Bison Workshop. A bison in an apron hammers LALR tables on an anvil.

There is: you write the **recipe** (the grammar) and a factory builds the **machine** (the parser in C). That factory is Bison, a compiler-compiler.
Picture an industrial bakery. You hand in an order form in **three parts**, separated by %%: **ingredients** (declarations), **method** (rules) and **notes** (extra C code).

'When this step is done, write down the total' → **semantic action** { $$ = $1 + $3; }
Supplier who delivers one ingredient at a time → **yylex** (Lexi, or Flex)
The pastry robot that follows the table → **yyparse**

PostgreSQL (gram.y), Bash (parse.y) and PHP still use Bison today. GCC used it too, but switched to hand-written recursive descent (C++ in GCC 3.4, C in 4.1) to get better error messages.

How Bison decides each shift/reduce conflict
The **rule's** precedence = that of its last terminal (or of the %prec)
The lookahead **token's** precedence = the line where it was declared
%right '-' by mistake: 8-3-2 becomes 8-(3-2) = 7. Subtraction has to be %left.
And with %right '^' for power, what's 2^3^2?
%right: on a tie, shift. The stack keeps 2^3 and shifts the second '^': 3^2 = 9 first, then 2^9 = 512. As in math.
Check it: 512. The %right '^' line comes last, so it binds tighter than * and +.
%nonassoc '<': 1+1<3 works (= 1), but try 1<2<3 in your head; it becomes a syntax error, on purpose.

Reading the file piece by piece
%{ ... %}: C code copied literally to the top of the generated parser

bison -d calc.y # generates calc.tab.c and calc.tab.h
flex calc.l # generates lex.yy.c
gcc calc.tab.c lex.yy.c -o calc
echo "2+3*4" | ./calc # prints: = 14
