My turn!
With %left '-', what's 8-3-2? And with %right '-'?
In the rule '-' expr %prec UMINUS, why the %prec?
Without it, the rule would inherit the precedence of the binary '-' (the rule's last terminal). With %prec UMINUS, it gets the precedence of the %right UMINUS line, the strongest.
In the game's mini-Bison, what does NOT go into the specification?
The %{ %} prologue, the third section with C code, %union/%type. The game already has a ready-made scanner (numbers become NUM, words become ID) and understands actions like $$ = expression;.
If the exam asks 'write the Yacc specification', don't forget: the two %%, a %token for each named token, the ';' at the end of each rule and the actions in braces.
Why leave the grammar ambiguous?
A provocative question: if ambiguity is bad, why does almost every Bison calculator use expr : expr '+' expr?
What's the unambiguous alternative?
Layers: expr → expr + term | term; term → term * fator | fator. It works, but it grows one layer per precedence level.
Layered version: zero conflicts, zero %left, and it still gives 14.
And what's the advantage of the ambiguous version + %left?
A short, readable grammar with fewer unit reductions (term → fator...). The precedence goes into a little table of declarations.
How does Bison know the precedence of a RULE?
By the last terminal on the right side (expr '*' expr → that of '*'), or by the %prec, if you write it.
And the lookahead's?
By the %left/%right/%nonassoc line where the token appears. Lines further down = stronger.
A shift/reduce conflict where the token has NO declared precedence. What does Bison do?
Stops compiling with an error
Picks shift and emits a conflict warning
Picks reduce
Yacc/Bison default: shift, with a warning ('conflicts: N shift/reduce'). For reduce/reduce, it picks the rule that appears first in the file.
Is that 'shift' default good for the dangling if-then-else?
It is! Shift on 'else' makes the else match the nearest if, which is what C and Java do. That's why many people accept this conflict (and declare it with %expect 1).
Two possible trees: whose else is it? Shift picks the inner if.
Why are reduce/reduce conflicts more dangerous?
Because 'take the first rule' is almost never what you wanted, and one of the rules may become unreachable. They usually point to a grammar design mistake.
You can turn on reports: bison -v calc.y generates calc.output with all the states and conflicts. It's the table you learned to build by hand!

General format of a .y file
%{ C code %}: copied to the start of the parser
%left / %right / %nonassoc t1 t2: same precedence on the line; later lines have higher precedence
%start s: start symbol (default: the left side of the first rule)
%union / %type <field>: types of the semantic values (default: int, via YYSTYPE)
**Rule:** head : body1 { action1 } | body2 { action2 } ;. In the action, $$ is the head's synthesized attribute and $i that of the i-th symbol in the body. An omitted action equals { $$ = $1; }.

conflict in ACTION[s, a] between shift and reduce by A → β:
 pa := precedence of token a
 pr := precedence of the rule (%prec, or the last terminal of β)
 if pa or pr undefined: shift (+ conflict warning)
 else if pa > pr: shift
 else if pa < pr: reduce
 else (tie):
 %left → reduce
 %right → shift
 %nonassoc → error
reduce/reduce conflict: reduce by the rule that appears first (+ warning)

SDD, attributes and type system
**Syntax-directed definition (SDD):** a context-free grammar + attributes associated with the symbols + semantic rules associated with the productions.
Kinds of attribute (for a nonterminal A at a node N)
**Synthesized:** defined by a rule of the production where A is the HEAD, using attributes of N's children and of N itself
**Inherited:** defined by a rule of the production where A is in the BODY (at N's parent), using attributes of the parent, the siblings and N itself
Terminals only have synthesized attributes, supplied by the scanner (e.g. num.lexval)
SDD classes
**S-attributed:** synthesized attributes only → post-order evaluation; implementable during LR parsing

**L-attributed:** in A → X1...Xn, each inherited attribute of Xi depends only on inherited attributes of A and on attributes of X1...Xi-1 (and of Xi, with no cycle) → a single depth-first pass, left to right
**Translation scheme (SDT):** a grammar with program fragments {actions} embedded in the body; in an S-attributed SDD, the actions go at the end (postfix SDT)
Classic L-attributed SDD: declarations (in is inherited)

Coercion = an implicit conversion done by the compiler. int → float is widening (it doesn't lose the order of magnitude). float → int would be narrowing and usually requires an explicit cast.
An instance of the rule above: max(int, float) = float, with widen on a.
When classifying an SDD, check EACH rule that defines an inherited attribute: does it use any sibling to the right? If so, it's not L-attributed. No inherited attributes → S-attributed (and also L).
Type checking is static (at compile time). Division by zero with variable values only shows up at runtime; it's not a type error.

x (3) is float and y (4) is int → float + int = float. The symbol table feeds type checking!

On the exam, draw the stack of tables next to the code and update it at each { and }. It's faster and avoids confusing who has already 'died'.
Wouldn't a single table be enough?
Let's design the symbol table together, with questions.
What information should be kept for each name?
At least: name, type, kind (variable, function, parameter...) and, later, address/offset in memory. Sometimes the declaration's line, for error messages.
Why doesn't a single global map name → information work?
Because the same name can have different declarations in different blocks (x int and x float). And when leaving a block, its names need to vanish.
So what do you do on entering a block? And on leaving?
Entering: create a new table, linked to the previous one. Leaving: go back to the previous one, throwing away the new one. A stack of tables!
And to look up a name, where do I start?
Where does the lookup start, and when does it stop?
It starts at the top table (innermost block) and goes down; it stops at the first match. If it reaches the bottom without finding it: 'undeclared'.
Declaring 'int x' when there's already an 'x' in an OUTER block is...
A redeclaration error
Allowed: the new x shadows the outer one
Ignored

The redeclaration check only looks at the TOP table. In different blocks, the new x shadows the old one (C and C++ allow it; Java, by design choice, forbids a local from shadowing another local, but the table works the same way).
Static (lexical) vs dynamic scope: what's the difference?
Static: the right x is decided by the program's TEXT (nesting). Dynamic: by the order of CALLS at runtime (the most recent active declaration). C, Java and Kotlin use static.
In which phase does the compiler use and fill in the table?
The scanner can insert the names; syntax/semantic analysis inserts declarations and resolves uses; code generation uses the addresses. It goes along with every phase.

The **scope** of a declaration: the region of the program in which a use of that name refers to it. **Most closely nested rule:** a use of x refers to the declaration of x in the innermost block that contains the use.

Dynamic follows the chain of CALLS: the most recent activation with x is g's. With static scope, f would see the global (1).

The recipe for the helper who does one thing at a time

Why not turn the tree straight into assembly?
Because there are dozens of processors. It's smarter to translate into a simple intermediate language, and only at the end into each machine.
Picture a recipe for a kitchen helper who can only do **one operation at a time**, with **at most two ingredients**, and always puts the result **in a labeled bowl**.
One operation at a time, two ingredients → **three-address instruction**: x = y op z
Bowls labeled t1, t2... → **temporaries** generated by the compiler
Recipe order → **post-order** of the tree: children before the parent

A card with no bowl: 'use the result of step 0' → **triple**

The smart shopping list
Code Forge, polishing room. TAC arrives a bit rough; here it leaves shining.
Does optimizing mean making the code OPTIMAL?
The name is misleading: it means **improving**, without changing the program's result. Truly 'optimal' is impossible to guarantee. Let's think of a shopping list.
Your list says: 'buy 2 × 6 eggs'. You do the math **at home**, not at the checkout: 12 eggs. That's **constant folding**: computing at compile time.
The list says 'buy milk' twice, and nothing changed in between. You buy it once and use it for both. That's eliminating a **common subexpression**.
The list has 'buy yeast', but no recipe uses it. Cut it! That's eliminating **dead code**.
Doing the math at home → **constant folding** (2 * 6 becomes 12)
Writing down 'eggs = 12' and using 12 from then on → **constant propagation**
Buying milk only once → **common subexpression elimination**
Crossing off the yeast nobody uses → **dead code elimination**
A stretch of the market with no turns, one way in and one way out → **basic block**
Which line can be computed entirely by the compiler?
Only 2 * 3 depends on constants alone. It becomes t1 = 6 before the program runs.
The generator produces t1 = 2 * 3; with constant folding, only one instruction is left: 6 + a.
Golden rule: optimization can NEVER change what the program does. When in doubt (side effects, division by zero...), the compiler doesn't optimize.
In the analogy, why can 'buy milk' twice become once only if 'nothing changed in between'?
If someone had drunk the milk in the middle (a redefined variable), the second purchase would be needed. A common subexpression only counts with no redefinition of the operands.

**Copy propagation:** (4) x = t2 * t2

Does the order matter? Can I do dead code first?
You can, but one optimization usually opens room for another. Compilers repeat the passes until nothing changes.

When is it safe to optimize?
Optimization has an oath: don't change the behavior. Let's test that oath with questions.
Can x = 10 / 0 be 'folded' by the compiler?
Not as a value: the division by zero has to happen (or be reported). The game's folder actually refuses to fold it.
And t = 0.1 + 0.2 with float?
It can, as long as the compiler uses exactly the same arithmetic as the target machine. Otherwise the result would change.
When are two occurrences of a + b the 'same' subexpression?
When neither a nor b was redefined between them (and there's no side effect, like a function call that changes a or b).
And dead code: how does the compiler know nobody uses it?
What does it mean for a variable to be 'alive' at a point?
That its value can be used later, on some execution path, before being redefined. An assignment to a variable that isn't alive is dead code.

Remove the whole block: it's unreachable code

With the condition constant, the jump always skips the block. Unreachable = it can go.
Why split the code into basic blocks before optimizing?
Inside a block there are no jumps in or out in the middle: the instructions all run, in order. It's easy to reason about values.
x * 2 → x + x or x << 1: what optimization is that?
Strength reduction: swapping an expensive operation for a cheaper equivalent one.

Basic blocks and semantics-preserving transformations

**Basic block:** a maximal sequence of consecutive instructions where the flow only enters through the first and only leaves through the last, with no jumps in the middle. **Flow graph:** blocks as nodes; edges to the possible successors.

LEADERS:
 1. the first instruction of the code is a leader
 2. every instruction that is the TARGET of a jump (conditional or not) is a leader
 3. every instruction that comes IMMEDIATELY AFTER a jump is a leader
BLOCKS:
 each leader starts a block, which goes up to the instruction
 before the next leader (or to the end)
Partitioning into basic blocks (Dragon Book, Alg. 8.5)
Classic transformations
**Constant folding:** evaluate at compile time operations with constant operands (2 * 3 → 6)
**Constant propagation:** after x = 6, replace uses of x with 6 as long as x isn't redefined
**Common subexpressions:** E already computed and operands not redefined since then → reuse the value
**Copy propagation:** after x = y, use y in place of x
**Dead code:** remove instructions whose result isn't alive (never used afterward)
**Strength reduction / loop-invariant code motion:** swap expensive ops; move out of the loop whatever doesn't change in it
**Local** = inside a basic block (e.g. via the block's DAG). **Global** = over the flow graph, with data-flow analysis (live variables, reaching definitions, available expressions).
Which transformation requires knowing which variables are ALIVE?
Dead code elimination
It's only safe to delete x = ... if x's value isn't used afterward. 'Alive' means exactly that.
Local constant folding: 3 * 4 → 12.
Classic question: 'identify the leaders and the basic blocks'. Mark leaders with the 3 rules, numbering the instructions; then draw the flow graph with both the jump edges AND the fall-through edges.
The instruction AFTER a jump is a leader, not the jump itself. The goto/if closes the block; it's the LAST instruction of the block.

The group in the group chat
A packed bus station, the day before a holiday. You and your friends need to get to the right platform, but the sign says: 'Bus A: platform 1 OR platform 3'. Where's the certainty?
I'd freeze. Do I pick one and hope?

An **NFA** does it differently: it doesn't choose. The group SPLITS UP and each one goes to a possibility. And there are open corridors, with no turnstile: whoever is at a point can cross for free. Those are the **ε** tracks.
Now the trick: instead of following each friend, you just look at the **group chat** and write down: 'right now the group is at {1, 3, 4}'. That whole set becomes ONE state of a **DFA**.
Bus station → subset construction
Each platform is an **NFA state**.
An open corridor (reading no letter) is an **ε transition**. Gathering everyone you can reach on foot is the **ε-closure**.
Using a ticket with the letter 'a' is **move(T, a)**: where each friend can go reading 'a'.
The group's list ('we're at {0, 1}') is a **DFA state**: a SET of NFA states.
If nobody in the group has anywhere to go, the group is empty: it's the **dead state ∅**.
If at least ONE friend reached the destination, the whole group celebrates: the set is **final** if it contains some NFA final state.
So the DFA is just the group's diary: 'we were here, we read such a letter, we ended up there'?
Exactly. And since the diary is written down BEFORE the trip, when reading the input there's no doubt anymore: one step per letter.
In the NFA for '(a|b)*ab' the group starts at {0}. From 0, reading 'a', you can stay at 0 or go to 1. Reading 'a', where does the group end up?
The group splits: some stay at 0, others go to 1. The DFA state is the set {0, 1}. No doubt, no lottery: we carry both possibilities together.
Move step by step: in yellow, where the group is. Notice the final DFA has only 3 states.

Q: If the NFA already recognizes the language, why convert it? A: Simulating the NFA means carrying a set with each letter read. The DFA does that work ONCE, during construction; after that, each character costs a single table lookup. A scanner reads millions of characters: those savings matter.
With 3 platforms, how many different lists could the group chat have, at most? Think of each platform as 'has people' or 'doesn't'.
2³ = 8 possible lists (including the empty one). That's why an NFA with n states becomes a DFA with up to 2ⁿ states. But the group almost always visits only a few lists; in the example above, 3.
In the analogy, who is: the platform, the open corridor, the group's list, the empty group?
An NFA state, an ε transition, a DFA state (a set of NFA states) and the dead state ∅.
Watching the subset factory
Today you'll SEE the construction happen. At each step, the yellow shows the current set, and the DFA table fills in by itself.
The classic (a|b)*abb, in an NFA version with 4 states. Go slowly.
Notice: we start at A = {0}. Reading 'a' we go to {0, 1} = B; from B, reading 'b', we go to {0, 2} = C; from C, reading 'b', we reach {0, 3} = D, the only one that contains the final state 3.
Why do ALL the DFA states contain 0?
Because 0 is the start state and never leaves the set
Because 0 has a loop on a and on b: whoever is at 0 can always stay at 0
Coincidence
Because 0 is final
The a,b loop at 0 means 'I haven't started the abb suffix yet'. That possibility never dies, so 0 shows up in every set.
Now with ε tracks. Here the first state is already NOT just {0}.
ab* | c: two ε tracks leave state 0. See the ε-closure right at the start.
In the NFA for 'ab* | c', 0 has ε tracks to 1 and to 3. What's ε-closure({0})?
The ε-closure includes 0 itself and everyone reachable by ε alone: 1 and 3. 2 and 4 require reading a letter, so they stay out.

When the move is empty (for example, from A = {0, 1, 3} reading 'b'), the widget shows ∅: it's the **dead state**. The DFA drawing leaves the dead state out, but it exists; any transition that doesn't show up leads there.
(ab | a)c: two paths that meet again via ε at state 4.
Notice the step from A on 'a': move = {1, 3}, but the ε-closure pulls in 4 too, because 3 --ε--> 4. Result: B = {1, 3, 4}. That's why 'ac' is accepted: B already 'knows' it can read the c.
How many states does the DFA for (ab | a)c have, and which one is final?
4 states: A = {0}, B = {1, 3, 4}, C = {2, 4} and D = {5}. Only D is final, because only it contains 5.
And when does the number of states really blow up?
'The third-to-last symbol is a'. The NFA has 4 states; the minimal DFA has 8 = 2³. It needs to remember the last 3 letters!
That kind of language is the worst case. Real token patterns (identifiers, numbers, keywords) produce small DFAs, which is why Lex/Flex can convert everything to a DFA without fear.
Subsets with ε, from start to finish
Let's slowly solve an NFA WITH ε transitions. That's how it shows up on the exam, because Thompson's NFA has ε everywhere.
Two paths (ab or a) that join at 4 before the c
The recipe has a single step, repeated: **Dtran[T, x] = ε-closure(move(T, x))**. First move with the letter (move), then move for free along the ε's (closure).
Start: A = ε-closure({0}) = {0}. No ε leaves 0.
A on b and A on c: move = ∅ → dead state.
B on b: move = {2}. Closure: 2 --ε--> 4, so **C = {2, 4}**.
D on any letter: ∅. No new state: done!
Finals: whoever contains 5 → only **D**. A DFA with 4 states (not counting the dead one).
Dtran table (→ start, * final, ∅ = dead state)
Check each row of the table with the engine.
Mistake #1 is forgetting the closure after the move. Without it, B would be {1, 3} and the DFA would reject 'ac', even though 'ac' is in the language!
Now it's up to you (faded example). NFA for **ab* | c**: 0 --ε--> 1, 0 --ε--> 3, 1 --a--> 2, 2 --b--> 2, 3 --c--> 4. Finals: 2 and 4.
What's the DFA's start state A?
A = ε-closure({0}) = {0, 1, 3}. Both ε's leave 0.
Compute Dtran[A, a], Dtran[A, b] and Dtran[A, c].
Continue with B = {2} and C = {4}. Which ones are final?
B on b: {2} = B (the b* loop). Everything else gives ∅. Finals: B (contains 2) and C (contains 4). A DFA with 3 states.

ALWAYS build the table with the columns 'DFA state | NFA set | one column per symbol'. Write the move and the closure separately on scratch paper: the professor gives partial credit for the reasoning.
Why sets?
Today I'll only ask. You'll reinvent the subset construction on your own.
An NFA is at state 0 and has TWO 'a' tracks: to 0 and to 1. Reading 'a', where is it?
At 0
At 1
At both at the same time
Stuck: an NFA can't have that
The NFA accepts if ANY path accepts. To not lose any, we follow all of them at once: the NFA is at {0, 1}.
So if I always write down the SET where it can be, I never need to guess?
Right! And if you give each set a name (A, B, C…), you just invented a deterministic automaton.
After reading a letter, why apply the ε-closure again?
You don't need to, only at the start
Because, on reaching a state, the NFA can move on for free along the ε tracks
To remove repeated states
To find the finals
An ε track doesn't consume input. If you reach 3 and there's 3 --ε--> 4, then you're also at 4. Forgetting that loses paths.
And when move(T, a) gives the empty set?
The string is accepted
We go back to the start state
We go to the dead state ∅, which you never leave
It's an error in the construction
No path survived. ∅ is a DFA state like any other, just non-final and with a loop on everything.
Should a set like {0, 2} be final when the NFA's final state is 2? And {0, 1}?
{0, 2} is final: ONE path reaching the end is enough. {0, 1} isn't: no path is at a final state.
Now the size. Look at this 3-state NFA: 'the second-to-last symbol is a'.
Count how many states the DFA gets.
With 3 states in the NFA, the maximum would be 2³ = 8 sets. Why did only 4 show up?
The engine made a mistake
Every reachable set contains 0 (because of the loop), so only 2² = 4 combinations are left
Because the NFA has no ε
Because the alphabet has 2 letters
0 is always present; only states 1 and 2 vary (in or out). That's 2 × 2 = 4 possible sets, and all of them show up.
If it were 'the n-th symbol from the end is a', how many states would the DFA have?
2ⁿ. The DFA needs to remember the last n letters, and each can be a or b. It's the classic example of exponential blowup.
n = 3: the minimal DFA has 2³ = 8 states. Not even minimizing gets you out of it.
So why do scanners use DFAs anyway?

Because the blowup is rare with real token patterns, the conversion happens ONCE (when generating the scanner) and after that each character costs a single step. Pay at the factory to save on the road.
Subset construction: exam definition
**NFA**: N = (S, Σ, δ, s₀, F), with δ: S × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → P(S). **DFA**: a special case with no ε transitions and exactly one destination for each (state, symbol) pair.

**ε-closure(s)**: states reachable from s using only ε transitions (includes s). **ε-closure(T)** = ∪ ε-closure(s), s ∈ T. **move(T, a)**: states reachable from some s ∈ T by ONE transition labeled a.

ε-closure(T):
 push all the states of T
 closure ← T
 while the stack isn't empty:
 pop t
 for each u with t --ε--> u:
 if u ∉ closure: closure ← closure ∪ {u}; push u
 return closure
Computing the ε-closure (Dragon Book, Fig. 3.33)
Subset construction (Algorithm 3.20)
**Correctness**: the DFA D simulates all the paths of the NFA N in parallel; after reading w, D is at T exactly when T is the set of states N can be in after reading w. So L(D) = L(N).
The book's example: Thompson's NFA for (a|b)*abb (states 0..10, final 10)
In the book's example, why is E the only final state?
Because it was the last one created
Because it's the only one that contains state 10, the NFA's final state
Because it has more states
Because Dtran[E, b] = C
Rule: T is final if T ∩ F ≠ ∅. F = {10} and only E contains 10.

Q: The book's DFA has 5 states, but the minimal DFA for (a|b)*abb has 4. Is it wrong? A: No! The subset construction doesn't guarantee the minimum. A and C behave the same (both go to B on a and to C on b) and minimization merges them.
The engine shows the DFA already minimized: 4 states.

**Cost**: an NFA with n states can produce a DFA with up to 2ⁿ states. Classic comparison for recognizing x with the regex r: simulating the NFA takes O(|r|) space and O(|r| × |x|) time; the DFA takes O(|x|) time, but may require O(2^|r|) space in the worst case.
Which statement is TRUE?
An NFA recognizes more languages than a DFA
Every NFA has an equivalent DFA, which may have exponentially more states
The subset construction always produces the minimal DFA
The DFA's start state is always {s₀}
Same power (regular languages), a possibly exponential size cost. The start state is ε-closure({s₀}), which can be bigger than {s₀}.

Classic question: 'convert Thompson's NFA for (a|b)*abb into a DFA'. Memorize the path: ε-closure({0}) = {0,1,2,4,7}, five states A–E, E final, and A ≡ C in minimization. Write Dtran[T, a] = ε-closure(move(T, a)) at the top of the sheet.
Write the algorithm's central formula and the rules for start and final states.
Dtran[T, a] = ε-closure(move(T, a)). Start: ε-closure({s₀}). Finals: every T that contains at least one NFA final state.
Move and Close the Door
**Move and close the door!** First MOVE with the letter (move), then CLOSE (ε-closure). Like your mom yelling from the kitchen: you came in, close the door!
**Fruit basket**: each DFA state is a basket with NFA states inside. The basket is **final if it has ONE prize fruit** (an NFA final state). The **empty basket ∅** is the dead state.

**Memory palace**: in the Lexical Forest, right after the Automaton Train, is the **Subset Factory** . Thompson's elves deliver messy tracks (NFA); the workers put states in baskets, stamp them A, B, C… and hand the train a map with no doubts (DFA).
**2ⁿ = light switches**: each NFA state is a lamp that's on (in the basket) or off. n lamps → 2ⁿ combinations. It's the CEILING, not the norm.
What's the correct order inside each step of the construction?
ε-closure, then move
move, then ε-closure
only move
only ε-closure
Move (move with the letter) and close the door (ε-closure). The ε-closure 'alone' shows up only once: at the start state, ε-closure({s₀}).
**The start state also closes the door**: the DFA's start state is NOT {s₀}, it's ε-closure({s₀}). If you forget, the basket starts out missing fruit.
a*b*: the start state is already {0, 1} because of the ε. Notice that A is already final; the empty string is accepted!

Contrasts that show up on exams: **move** uses ONE letter; **ε-closure** uses no letter at all. An **NFA** can be in several states; a **DFA** in exactly one. **∅** is the dead state, not the start state. Subsets do NOT minimize: that's another step.

The whole conveyor: **T**hompson **T**ransforms (regex → NFA), **S**ubsets **S**implify (NFA → DFA), **M**inimization **M**erges the repeated ones (DFA → minimal DFA). Lex/Flex run the whole conveyor for you.
Without looking: the 3 rules of the subset construction.
1) Start = ε-closure({s₀}). 2) Dtran[T, a] = ε-closure(move(T, a)): move and close the door. 3) T is final if it contains some NFA final state.
Why do scanners prefer DFAs?
One step per character, with no backtracking and no sets to carry. The (possibly expensive) conversion is done only once, when the scanner is generated.
The post office sorting center
A post office sorting center, at dawn. An endless conveyor of characters passes in front of a robot. Lexi holds a laminated sheet full of rules.
I don't sort anything by hand. I write the RULE SHEET, hand it to the factory, and the factory builds the robot that does the sorting on its own.
The rule sheet ('package like this → such a stamp') is the **.l file**: each line is a **pattern** (regular expression) and an **action** in C.
The factory that reads the sheet and builds the robot is the **lex** (or **flex**) program: it generates the file **lex.yy.c**.
The robot is the function **yylex()**: each time someone calls it, it takes the next package and returns the stamp.
The package the robot took is the **lexeme**: it's in **yytext**, and its length in **yyleng**.
The stamp is the action's **return TOKEN;**. An empty action **{ }** is the trash bin: spaces and comments vanish.

The robot obeys TWO golden rules. First: it's **greedy**: it always takes the BIGGEST package some rule accepts. Second: if two rules accept packages of the same size, the one **higher up on the sheet** wins.
See which rule stamped each lexeme. Edit the input and test it!
With this sheet ("if" above the identifier rule), what does 'iffy' become?
IF followed by ID 'fy'
A single ID 'iffy'
Greedy! The ID rule accepts 4 characters; the "if" one only 2. The biggest package wins, and the order isn't even checked.
And if someone pastes the ID rule ABOVE the "if" rule?
Sheet with the order swapped: look at what happened to 'if'.
Why did 'if' become ID?
A tie: both rules accept 'if' with 2 characters. On a tie the one that comes FIRST wins, and now that's ID. Keywords ALWAYS come before the identifier rule.

In the course project, the scanner is usually done like this: you write scanner.l, run `lex scanner.l && gcc lex.yy.c` and test with `./a.out < programa.txt`. lex writes hundreds of lines of C for you.

Q: Are Lex and Flex the same thing? A: Flex ('fast lex') is the free, faster version of the original Lex. The .l syntax is practically the same; on many Linux systems, the `lex` command already calls flex.
In the analogy, who is: the sheet, the factory, the robot, the package and the stamp?

The REAL rule matches '3.14' (4 characters) and the NUM one only '3' (1 character). Longest match wins, even with NUM coming later on the sheet.
The '@' falls into the catch-all rule '.', which prints the error and does NOT return a token. The scanner keeps going.
The '.' rule has to be the LAST one. It matches any character with length 1; if it came earlier, it would win every length-1 tie, and swallow `+`, `;` and even one-letter identifiers!

Only 1: ID 'ab'. 'x' and '+' have length 1 and tie with '.', which comes first and throws them away. 'ab' has length 2 and the '.' can't reach it.

Check the damage.
How does Flex manage to find the LONGEST match among dozens of rules at once?

It joins the NFAs of all the rules into one (a new start state with ε to each one), converts it to a DFA and runs the DFA until it gets stuck in the dead state, remembering the LAST final state it went through. That final state gives the lexeme's length and the rule (the one with the lowest number, on a tie).
And why is the result so fast?
Because it's a DFA: one step per character, one table lookup. All the hard work (subsets, minimization) was paid when lex generated lex.yy.c.
The Lex specification: exam definition

A Lex program has three sections separated by `%%`: **declarations** (C code between `%{` and `%}` and regular definitions name → regex), **translation rules** in the form `Pattern { Action }` and **auxiliary functions** in C.

declarations
%%
translation rules
%%
auxiliary functions
Structure of a .l file

EXPRESSION MATCHES EXAMPLE
c the character c (not an operator) a
\c the character c literally \*
"s" the string s literally "**"
. any character but \n a.*b
^ start of line ^abc
$ end of line abc$
[s] any character in s [abc]
[^s] any character not in s [^abc]
r* zero or more r a*
r+ one or more r a+
r? zero or one r a?
r{m,n} m to n occurrences of r a{1,5}
r1r2 r1 followed by r2 ab
r1|r2 r1 or r2 a|b

Lex regular expressions (Dragon Book, Fig. 3.8)

**Conflict resolution** (Dragon Book, 3.5.3): (1) always prefer the **longest prefix** of the input that matches some pattern; (2) if the longest prefix matches two or more patterns, prefer the **one listed first**.
Interface of the generated scanner
**yylex()**: returns the code of the next token; returns 0 at the end of the input.
**yytext**: a pointer to the start of the recognized lexeme; **yyleng**: its length.
**yylval**: a global variable with the token's attribute value, shared with the parser (Yacc/Bison).
**yyin**: the input file (default: stdin). **yywrap()**: called at the end of the file; returning 1 means 'done'.

**Implementation**: Lex builds an NFA for each pattern pᵢ, creates a new start state with ε transitions to each one, and converts the combined NFA into a DFA. When reading the input, the DFA goes on until there's no transition; then it backs up to the last accepting state seen. If that state contains finals of several patterns, the one with the lowest index counts.
the "if" token and then the lexeme 'a'
a single lexeme 'ifa', from the rule [a-z]+
error: conflict
Resolution rule 1: longest prefix. [a-z]+ matches 3 characters; "if" matches 2.
What's the role of the `/` operator in `DO/({letra}|{digito})*=…`?
Division
Lookahead: it only matches DO if what comes after matches the rest, but the rest doesn't go into the lexeme
A comment
An alternative, like |
It's the right-context (lookahead) operator, used in the Fortran example, where DO5I=1.25 is an assignment and DO5I=1,25 is a loop.

In an essay question: mention the 3 sections, the 2 conflict resolution rules (longest; tie → first) and explain that Lex generates a DFA from the regexes (Thompson + subsets). Bonus: keywords before identifiers.
Write the rule for an identifier that returns ID and keeps the name for the parser.
[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]* { yylval.nome = strdup(yytext); return ID; }; strdup copies it, because yytext will be overwritten on the next token.
Greedy, but polite
**D-R-C**: **D**efinitions %% **R**ules %% **C**ode. Just like Bison: Declare, Rule, Code. The two %% are the two walls of the rules room.
Flex is **greedy, but polite**: GREEDY because it always eats the biggest piece; POLITE because, on a tie, it respects the line: whoever got to the file first is served.
**A keyword is VIP**: it goes BEFORE the ID on the sheet. If the ID cuts in front, 'if' becomes a variable and your project breaks.

**Memory palace**: in the Lexical Forest, on the riverbank, is the **Flex Workshop** . The D-R-C sheet is nailed to the door. Inside, Lexi feeds the machine regular expressions and out the other side comes a robot called lex.yy.c.

Everything in lex starts with **yy**: **yytext** = the lexeme's TEXT; **yyleng** = its LENGth; **yylval** = the VALue that goes to Bison; **yylex** = the LEXer itself; **yywrap** = 'wrap it up' (is the file over?).
**Empty { } = trash bin.** Without return, the lexeme goes to the trash and the robot keeps going. That's how spaces and comments vanish.
yytext or yylval: where is the text "42" right after matching `[0-9]+`?
yytext is the raw TEXT. yylval only has the value if YOUR action does yylval = atoi(yytext).
Greedy: 'iffy' and 'while2' are IDs. Polite: for 'if' alone, the top rule would win.

Classic mix-ups: (1) thinking order settles EVERYTHING; length comes first; (2) putting the '.' rule at the start; (3) forgetting yywrap/noyywrap; (4) returning the space token instead of ignoring it; (5) mixing up lex.l (what you write) with lex.yy.c (what lex generates).
Recite the two golden rules and the mnemonic for the sections.
1) Longest match (greedy). 2) Tie → the rule listed first (polite). Sections: D-R-C, Definitions %% Rules %% Code.
The essay grader
A pile of 300 essays and a cold coffee. On line 3 of the first one, the grader finds a mistake.
So he tears up the essay and leaves?
Of course not! He marks the mistake, finds a safe point to continue, the next period, and keeps reading. In the end, the student gets ALL the mistakes at once. A good compiler does the same.
Kinds of errors, in the essay and in the code
'Hous' instead of 'house' → **lexical error**: a character or word that doesn't exist (in C, a stray `@`).
A sentence with no verb, an unclosed parenthesis → **syntax error**: the structure is broken (`x = (a + ;`).
'The sun froze the stew' → **semantic error**: structure OK, meaning not (adding a string to an int, an undeclared variable).
A perfect text, but off topic → **logic error**: it compiles and runs, but does the wrong thing (`if (x = 0)` instead of `==`).
The grader's four strategies
**Panic mode**: skip everything until the next period and start again from there. Simple and never loops; but it can skip a big stretch.
**Phrase level**: make a local patch, 'a comma is missing here, I'll pretend it's there'. Careful: badly chosen patches can create infinite loops.
**Error productions**: the answer key already predicts the most common mistakes and has a ready message for each.
**Global correction**: rewrite the essay with the MINIMUM changes until it's right. Beautiful in theory, too expensive in practice.
Which of these strategies do real compilers use most?
Global correction
Panic mode (sometimes with phrase-level patches)
None: they stop at the first error
Error productions for every possible error
Panic is simple and safe. Global correction is too expensive; error productions only for frequent cases.
In my Temple, the 'period' is called a **sync token**. In C, the favorites are `;` and `}`.

With the terminal ';' on top of the stack and 'id' in the input, it pretends the ';' was there: it pops the ';' and keeps going. It's a phrase-level patch, exactly the grader's 'I'll pretend the comma is here'.
Grader: 'I don't fix the essay, I just point things out.' Compiler: 'Me too! Recovering isn't fixing the program: it's just getting back to a state where I can find the NEXT error.'
In the analogy, who is: the period, the patch, the answer key of common mistakes and the minimal rewrite?
The sync token (panic mode), phrase-level recovery, error productions and global correction.
Panic Room live
Welcome to the Panic Room. The red token is where I NOTICE the error. Then move step by step and watch how I recover.
Grammar: a list of assignments. FIRST(E) = {id, num}, FOLLOW(E) = {;}
One '=' too many. With E on top and '=' in the input, cell M[E, =] is empty.
Panic rule: with the nonterminal A on top and an empty cell, **drop tokens** until you find one that (1) is in **FIRST(A)**: then A stays on top, or (2) is in **FOLLOW(A) ∪ {$}**: then A is popped.
In the example above, the parser drops the '=' and finds 'num'. What does it do?
Pops E
Continues with E, because num ∈ FIRST(E)
Gives up
Goes back to the start of the program

The ';' doesn't start an E, but it's in FOLLOW(E): it's what would come right AFTER an E. The parser 'gives up' on E and syncs on the ';'.

A terminal on top different from the input: the parser pretends the terminal was there and pops it. It's a simple phrase-level recovery (an 'insertion').

ONE typo caused TWO recoveries: first the parser pretends there's a ';' and then it drops 'num ;'. That's the **cascading error**: that's why, after the first error, be suspicious of the following messages.

In the expression grammar: the '*' shows up where a term T should start.
Which token is dropped in 'id + * id', and why?
The '*'. With T on top, M[T, *] is empty; '*' isn't in FIRST(T) = {(, id} or in FOLLOW(T) = {+, ), $}. The next one, 'id', is in FIRST(T): the parser goes on with T.
Tracing panic by hand
Let's slowly trace panic mode on `id = ; id = num ;`: the programmer forgot the value of the first assignment.
Solved (top of the stack on the right)
M[E, ;] is empty → **error detected at the 3rd token**. Message: 'expected id or num, found ;'.
Panic: ';' ∉ FIRST(E), but ';' ∈ FOLLOW(E). Nothing to drop: **pop E**.
Stack `$ P ;`: match `;`. The rest, `id = num ;`, is parsed normally.
At the end, P → ε with `$` and the parser reaches the end: 1 error reported, complete analysis.
Check each step with the engine.
After an error, the parser does NOT generate code: recovery is only for continuing to look for errors. The program only really compiles when the list of errors is empty.
At which token is the error detected, and what's on top of the stack?
At the 3rd token, the second '='. On top is E (we already matched id and =).
What does panic do?
'=' isn't in FIRST(E) or in FOLLOW(E): drop '='. The next one, 'num', is in FIRST(E): stop dropping and go on with E → num.
The error shows up with the TERMINAL '=' on top and 'num' in the input. The parser pretends the '=' was there (pops the '=') and goes on with E → num.
Check the last answer.

parser.y: 'error ;' drops everything up to the next ';' and moves on to the next statement

Why not stop at the first error?
Questions, only questions. You'll deduce how a compiler should react to errors.
Your program has 5 syntax errors. The compiler stops at the first one. How many times do you compile until you find them all?
At least 5
It depends on the processor
One error per compilation = at least 5 rounds. That's why the compiler tries to recover and report as many errors as possible at once.
At the 1st (id)
At the 3rd (the first num)
At the 4th (the second num)
Only at the end
'id = num' can still become a valid program (just add a ';'). The 2nd 'num' is the first token that makes that impossible.
The red marks the detection point.
It shouts exactly at the first impossible token. Does that have a name?
It does: the **viable prefix property**. LL and LR detect the error as soon as what has been read can no longer be the start of any valid program.
With E on top and an unexpected token, why use FOLLOW(E) as the sync set?
Because it's the smallest set
Because if the next token is something that comes AFTER an E, you can pretend the E ended and move on
Because FIRST is always empty
Popping E and continuing with what comes after it is the safest bet: the stack matches the input again.
And why also stop at a token in FIRST(E)?
Because then you can restart the E itself, without throwing away the rest
It shouldn't stop
To generate more errors
Because FIRST = FOLLOW
In `id = = num`, after dropping the extra '=', 'num' starts an E: there's no reason to abandon the E.
Why are ';' and '}' great sync tokens in C?
Because they mark clear ENDS of constructs (statement and block). Skipping to them usually drops only the broken statement, and the rest of the program is parsed normally.
What's the risk of syncing in the wrong place?
Cascading errors: the parser comes back 'misaligned' and reports errors that don't exist. That's why compilers wait for a few correct tokens before reporting the next error (Bison waits for 3).
Challenge: before moving on, predict whether the ')' will be dropped or used as a sync token for T.
Answer to the challenge
Sync token: ')' ∈ FOLLOW(T) = {+, ), $}. Nothing is dropped, T is popped and the ')' closes the parenthesis normally.
Handling syntax errors: exam definition

**Goals of the error handler** (Dragon Book, 4.1.3): (1) report the presence of errors clearly and accurately; (2) recover from each error quickly enough to detect subsequent errors; (3) add minimal overhead to the processing of correct programs.

**Viable prefix property**: LL and LR methods detect an error as soon as the prefix of the input already read can't be completed into a string of the language. The error is reported at the FIRST token that makes that impossible.
Recovery strategies
**Panic mode**: discard input symbols, one by one, until finding a **sync token** from a chosen set (e.g. `;`, `}`, FOLLOW(A)). Simple and free of infinite loops.
**Phrase level**: local correction of the rest of the input: insert, delete or replace a token (e.g. insert a missing `;`). A risk of looping if it always inserts before the current token.
**Error productions**: augment the grammar with productions that generate the most common wrong constructs, emitting specific diagnostics.
**Global correction**: find the correct string y closest to the input x (minimum insertions, deletions and swaps). Of theoretical interest: the cost is too high.

with A (nonterminal) on top and a = next token:
 if M[A, a] has a production: expand normally
 else: // error
 report the error (line, expected × found)
 while a ∉ FIRST(A) and a ∉ FOLLOW(A) ∪ {$}:
 discard a; a ← next token
 if a ∈ FIRST(A): continue with A on top
 else: pop A // synced on FOLLOW(A)
with terminal t on top and t ≠ a:
 report "expected t"; pop t // pretend t was there
Panic mode in the LL(1) parser (Dragon Book, 4.4.5)
Every empty cell in this table is an error point. The FOLLOW(A) columns are each row's 'synch' cells.
In the book's table, a cell M[A, a] marked 'synch' means:
Discard a
Pop A, since a ∈ FOLLOW(A)
Accept the input
Expand A → ε
Blank cell → discard the token. 'synch' → pop A. A terminal on top different from the token → pop the terminal.

**In Yacc/Bison**: the reserved token `error` can appear in productions, like `comando : error ';'`. On detecting an error, the parser calls **yyerror**, pops states until one that has an action for `error`, pushes `error` and discards tokens until one that can follow it. To avoid cascades, it only reports the next error after 3 tokens have been shifted successfully; **yyerrok** ends that mode right away and **yyclearin** discards the current token.
Which is NOT a goal of the error handler?
Reporting errors clearly
Detecting subsequent errors
Fixing the program automatically so it runs
Minimal cost on correct programs
Recovering ≠ fixing. Recovery is for continuing the analysis and finding more errors; no code is generated.

It shows up a lot: 'list and explain the error recovery strategies'. Write all four, with one advantage and one disadvantage each, and say that panic mode uses FOLLOW (and FIRST) as sync sets. Mention the viable prefix property.
Define the viable prefix property in one sentence.
The parser detects the error as soon as the prefix read from the input stops being a prefix of some sentence of the language, never later than that.
FIRST stays, FOLLOW flees
**FIRST stays, FOLLOW flees.** Found a token in FIRST(A)? A STAYS on top and starts over. Found one in FOLLOW(A)? A FLEES (it's popped). Neither? Throw the token away.
**Stubborn terminal? Pretend it was there.** A terminal on top that doesn't match the input is popped, like skipping a forgotten comma.

**Memory palace**: in the Top-Down Temple, behind the LL(1) table's altar, there's a door with a red light: the **Panic Room** . Stack runs through it throwing tokens out the window until he sees an exit sign, `;` or `}`, painted in FOLLOW's colors.

Kinds of errors in growing zoom: **Letter → Sentence → Meaning → Result**. Lexical (a word that doesn't exist), syntactic (a badly built sentence), semantic (a meaningless sentence), logical (everything compiles, but the result comes out wrong).
Strategies, from the simplest to the most ambitious: **P**anic **P**ounces, **P**hrase **P**atches, **P**roduction **P**redicts, **G**lobal is a **G**enius, but nobody pays its salary.
E on top, token 'x' in the input, x ∉ FIRST(E) and x ∉ FOLLOW(E). What do you do?
Pop E
Drop x and look at the next token
Push x
Neither stays nor flees: the token goes out the window. Repeat until you find someone in FIRST (stays) or in FOLLOW (flees).
Recite as you go: the junk '= = ;' goes out the window until 'id' shows up, which is in FIRST(P). P stays!
**Viable prefix = an immediate shout**: LL and LR shout at the FIRST impossible token, never later. If the message points to line 10, the real error is on line 10 or BEFORE.
Bison: **`error` is the wildcard** that matches the junk; **yyerrok** is 'OK, you can complain again'; **yyerror** is the megaphone that prints the message.

Classic mix-ups: (1) thinking recovering = fixing the program; (2) using FIRST as the 'pop' set (it's FOLLOW!); (3) forgetting the $ among the sync tokens; (4) blindly trusting the 2nd, 3rd… message; it may be a cascade.
Recite: what do you do with A on top and an empty cell?
Drop tokens until finding one in FIRST(A), A stays, or in FOLLOW(A) ∪ {$}, A flees (pop). FIRST stays, FOLLOW flees.
A good message has the line and 'expected × found': 'Syntax error on line 7: expected ';' but found 'id''. That's what the professor wants to see in your project.

.text
 main: li §a0, 3 # argument: n = 3
 jal fat # calls fat; §ra = address of the line below
 move §a0, §v0 # the result arrives in §v0
 li §v0, 1 # syscall 1: print integer
 syscall # prints 6
 li §v0, 10 # syscall 10: exit
 syscall

 fat: addi §sp, §sp, -8 # PROLOGUE: opens the frame (2 words)
 sw §ra, 4(§sp) # saves the return address
 sw §a0, 0(§sp) # saves n
 slti §t0, §a0, 2 # §t0 = (n < 2)
 beq §t0, §zero, REC # n >= 2? go to the recursion
 li §v0, 1 # base case: returns 1
 addi §sp, §sp, 8 # closes the frame
 jr §ra
 REC: addi §a0, §a0, -1 # argument n - 1
 jal fat # §v0 = fat(n - 1)
 lw §a0, 0(§sp) # gets back ITS n
 lw §ra, 4(§sp) # gets back ITS return address
 addi §sp, §sp, 8 # EPILOGUE: closes the frame
 mul §v0, §a0, §v0 # n * fat(n - 1)
 jr §ra # goes back to the caller
The kitchen's stack of plates
Code Forge, end of the shift. The code has been generated... but when it RUNS, where do each function's variables live?
In memory, duh. Each variable has its own fixed little spot, doesn't it?
Almost! Think of a restaurant kitchen on a busy day. Each order that starts becomes a plate on the stack on the counter, with a note stuck to it.

The note says: **which ingredients** came with the order, **which table** to return the finished plate to, and it has room for the cook's **scribbles**. And the cook only works on the plate on **top**.

If, in the middle of a plate, the cook needs a sauce that's another recipe, they put a **new plate on top**, make the sauce, take that plate off and go back to the one below exactly where they left off.
Each order in progress → an **activation** (a function call in progress)
Plate with a note → **activation record** (or **frame**)
The order's ingredients → **parameters**
The cook's scribbles → **local variables** and **temporaries**
Stack of plates on the counter → **runtime stack**: only the top works
A sauce that needs another sauce of the SAME recipe → **recursion**: several identical plates stacked
A new plate... goes on top. A finished plate... comes off the top. I never... take from the middle.
Recursive factorial: a recipe that asks for itself
Running fat(3), how many plates (activation records) are stacked at the HIGHEST moment, counting main's?
main → fat(3) → fat(2) → fat(1): four frames at the same time. Only when fat(1) returns 1 does the stack start going down. If you guessed 3, you forgot main's plate, a super common mistake!
Push and pop: each fat(n) has ITS OWN n on the note.
'If all the frames belong to the same function fat, why doesn't the n get mixed up?' Because each call gets a NEW plate, with its own n. The n=3 stays tucked away below while n=1 works on top.

And the rest of the kitchen? The **menu** pinned to the wall is the **code**; the **fixed signs** (the restaurant's name, opening hours) are the **static area** (global variables); the **storeroom**, where boxes are taken and returned at any time, is the **heap** (`new`, `malloc`).
Why does the storeroom (heap) exist, if the stack already works so well?
Because the stack's plate is thrown away when the function ends. If you need something that lives AFTER the return (an object created with `new`, a list that grows), it goes to the heap.
Recursion with no base case = plates stacked up to the ceiling. In Java that's the famous `StackOverflowError`; in C, usually a *segmentation fault*. It's the plate hitting the chandelier.
The call stack, frame by frame
Today we watch memory during execution. First, a program without recursion: main calls f, which calls g, which calls h.
f calls g, g calls h... and f calls h again
What you just saw
main calls f(1): stack [main, f]
f calls g(1): [main, f, g]
g calls h(2): [main, f, g, h], the highest point, 4 frames
f calls h(1) AGAIN: [main, f, h], the same h, a brand-new frame
h showed up twice, at different heights of the stack!
Exactly. The frame depends on WHO called and WHEN, not just on the function's name. That's why each frame keeps its own return address.

main + fat(4) + fat(3) + fat(2) + fat(1) = 5. Rule of thumb: recursion depth + 1 (main).

The activation tree tells the whole story; the stack shows only the 'now'. Walking the tree depth-first (going down = call, going up = return) is exactly what the stack does.

Why a STACK?
Let's reinvent the runtime environment with questions alone. Answer in your head before tapping; getting it wrong here is part of the method.
The simplest idea: each variable of each function gets a fixed address (static allocation). What goes wrong with fat(3)?

There's only ONE n for the function fat. When fat(2) writes n=2, it destroys the n=3 that fat(3) will still use on the way back. Static allocation doesn't support recursion (old FORTRAN didn't even allow recursion because of that).
So each CALL needs its own copy of n. In what order are those copies born and do they die?
The last call to start is the first to finish (LIFO): fat(1) is born last and dies first. That's exactly how a stack behaves.
OK, but besides n, what else does the frame need to keep?
When fat(1) finishes, how does the machine know where to go back to?
And how do you return the result and go back to using the caller's frame?
Who should OPEN the space for a function's LOCAL variables?
The caller, because it knows how many parameters it passes
The callee, because only it knows how many locals and temporaries it has
The operating system

The size of the locals is the callee's 'secret' (the caller may even have been compiled earlier). General rule: the caller takes care of what it knows (parameters, return address); the callee takes care of the rest.
A function creates a list and returns it to the caller. Can the list live in its frame?
No! The frame is popped on return, and the caller would be left with a pointer to garbage (a dangling pointer). Things that need to outlive the call go to the **heap**.
Infinite recursion: what happens to the stack?
Each call pushes a frame and none leaves. The stack grows until it invades a forbidden area: **stack overflow**.
And passing a parameter by reference? Does anything change in the frame?
In swap(x, y) by VALUE, what goes into the frame? And by REFERENCE?
By value: COPIES of x and y; swapping the copies changes nothing outside. By reference: the ADDRESSES of x and y; the callee writes directly into the caller's variables, and the swap really happens.

**Runtime environment**: the set of structures the generated code uses to run: memory organization, activation records, calling sequences and parameter passing.

Activation record (frame): typical fields (section 7.2.2)
Calling and return sequence
**Caller:** records the return address and the control link; jumps to the callee (`jal`)
**Caller:** retrieves the returned value and goes on

**Activation tree:** each node is an activation; a node's children are the activations it called, from left to right, in call order. **Property:** the control stack, at any given instant, contains exactly the path from the root to the node being executed.
Three allocation strategies
**Static:** a fixed address at compile time; allows neither recursion nor dynamic size (globals; FORTRAN 77)
**Stack:** one frame per activation, LIFO; allows recursion; the frame dies on return (locals in C and Java)
**Heap:** blocks with arbitrary lifetimes; manual freeing (`free`) or garbage collection

 §t0–§t9 temporaries: the CALLER saves them if needed later

Control/dynamic = the chain of CALLS. Access/static = the chain of NESTING in the text (useful in languages with nested functions, like Pascal). The return address points to an INSTRUCTION, not a frame.

The memory building and the frame's breakfast
Memory Palace: Code Forge, second-to-last room. A four-story building; from the roof, a stack of boxes comes down on its own.

**The building, from the bottom up: C-S-H-S ('Cats Sleep, Hamsters Spin').** **C**ode on the ground floor, **S**tatic on the 1st floor, **H**eap going up from the 2nd, **S**tack coming down from the roof.
**'Heap goes up, stack comes down; if they meet, the building falls.'** That's running out of memory.
**Control is for Calls, Access is for nesting.** **C**ontrol link → who **c**alled me (dynamic chain). **A**ccess link → where I'm nested in the text (static chain).

**The frame's breakfast, from top to bottom: 'Please Return Cold Apples, Since Lunch's Tomorrow'** → **P**arameters, **R**eturn value, **C**ontrol link, **A**ccess link, **S**aved status (return address), **L**ocals, **T**emporaries.
And how do I remember who does what in the call? I always mix them up.

Hotel reception! The **guest** (caller) arrives with the luggage and says when they're going home: parameters and return address. The **hotel** (callee) sets up the room and the minibar: locals and saved registers. On checkout, the hotel hands over the bill (return value) and frees the room.
In main → f → g → h (h called by g), by the hook 'Control is for Calls', h's control link points to the frame of...
Control = who CALLED. Whoever called h was g. (And when f calls h directly, the control link of that OTHER h frame points to f.)
Go up and down the building: each floor of the stack is a frame.
Recite the frame's 7 fields with the breakfast sentence.
Please Return Cold Apples, Since Lunch's Tomorrow → parameters, return value, control link, access link, saved status (return address), locals, temporaries.

Stack: 'I'm fast and tidy: in, out, all clean.' Heap: 'And I'm flexible: I keep whatever you want for as long as you want.' Stack: 'And you forget to give it back...' Heap: 'That's why they invented the garbage collector!'

Why so many lw's and sw's?
I'll only ask questions. You'll discover on your own how MIPS code is generated.
In MIPS, `add` only accepts registers. So how do you add two variables that are in memory?
First bring them into registers (lw), add, and return the result to memory (sw). MIPS is a **load/store** architecture: only lw/sw touch memory; everything else works in registers.

A `j` BACKWARD, back to the test label. The test sits at the start: if it fails, a FORWARD jump leaves the loop.

Why not put EVERYTHING in registers? Because there are only 32 (and several are reserved). When they run out, someone goes back to memory: the famous **spill**. Choosing well who stays is a hard problem (it becomes graph coloring!).

The servers who do the same thing
The neighborhood snack bar, lunchtime. The owner looks at the payroll and frowns: 'Five servers... do I need all of them?'
Huh, fire whoever works the least?

Not quite. He runs a test: he gives the same sequence of orders to two servers. If, for ANY sequence, both end up the same way (delivering the sandwich or not), they're **interchangeable**. He can merge both into a single position.
Each server is a DFA **state**.
Each customer order ('a', 'b') is an input **symbol**: the server passes you on to someone.
'Delivering the sandwich' at the end of the line of orders is ending in a **final state**.
Two servers who ALWAYS end the same way are **equivalent** (indistinguishable).
If there's ONE sequence of orders where one delivers and the other doesn't, they're **distinguishable**.
Merging all the equivalent ones gives the **minimal DFA**: the same service, a smaller payroll.
And in the Lexical Forest this matters a lot: my scanner is a giant DFA. Fewer states = a smaller table = a lighter scanner.
Yes, if they pass the orders on to the same people
No: with an EMPTY line one delivers and the other doesn't
It depends on the size of the alphabet
The empty string already separates them. That's why the first step of the method is always to mark every (final, non-final) pair: they're distinguishable right away.
Then comes the 'domino effect': if X and Y, on receiving 'b', pass you on to two servers we ALREADY know are different, then X and Y are different too.

q0 and q2 (in the book, A and C). Both send 'a' to q1 and 'b' to q2: they do exactly the same job. The DFA drops from 5 to 4 states.

How do you prove two states are different?
Today you'll invent the table method by answering questions. Start here: what does it mean for two states to be 'equal'?
What's the best definition of 'p and q are equivalent'?
They have the same arrows leaving them
For EVERY string w, reading w from p ends in a final state if and only if reading w from q also does
They're both final
They're close to each other in the drawing
Equivalence is about future BEHAVIOR: no string can separate the two. Having the same arrows is sufficient, but not necessary.
But 'for every string' is infinitely many strings! How do I test that?
Good one! Turn the question inside out: instead of proving they're equal, try to prove they're **different**. For that, ONE string is enough: a witness.
What's the shortest possible witness, and who does it separate?
'a', it separates whoever has a loop
The empty string ε: it separates every final from every non-final
'ab', it separates the start states
Reading nothing, you're already at the end. If p is final and q isn't, ε is the witness. Hence round 1.
Suppose {r, s} is already marked with witness w. If δ(p,'b') = r and δ(q,'b') = s, what's the witness for {p, q}?
'b' followed by w
w followed by 'b'
There isn't one
From p, reading 'b' leads to r; then w separates r from s. So 'b'w separates p from q. That's the 'domino effect': each round creates witnesses one letter longer.
Why does the algorithm need to repeat the rounds until nothing changes?
Because marking a new pair can make it possible to mark others that depended on it. In the book's DFA, {q0,q1} only falls in round 3, after {q2,q3} was marked in round 2.
Why does the algorithm always end?
There's a finite number of pairs, and a marked pair is never unmarked. Each useful round marks at least one; when a round marks nothing, the following ones wouldn't either.
A pair survived every round unmarked. What can we conclude?
Maybe they're different, by a long string we didn't test
They're equivalent: if a witness existed, some round would have found it
We need to test it by hand
The algorithm is complete: a witness of length n would be found in round n + 1. Unmarked at the end = no witness exists.
And if a transition is missing? What do I compare it with?

Complete the DFA with the dead state ∅ (non-final, a loop on everything) and compare normally. A missing transition means 'goes to the dead state'; ∅ is what makes it possible to mark pairs like {q1,q2} in a*b*.
Watch the witness 'a' separate q2 from q1 thanks to ∅.

State q0: 'q2 and I have done exactly the same job for years.' State q2: 'Right, nobody has ever found a string that tells us apart.' Minimizer: 'Then congratulations, you just became a single state.'
Minimization: exam definition
Let D = (S, Σ, δ, s₀, F) be a **complete** DFA with all states reachable. Extend δ to strings: δ*(p, ε) = p and δ*(p, xw) = δ*(δ(p, x), w).

**Equivalence**: p ≡ q if, for every w ∈ Σ*, δ*(p, w) ∈ F ⇔ δ*(q, w) ∈ F. Otherwise, p and q are **distinguishable**, and a w that separates them is a **witness**. ≡ is an equivalence relation; its classes are the states of the minimal DFA.
Table-filling algorithm (distinguishable pairs)

**Building the minimum**: states = classes [p]; δ'([p], c) = [δ(p, c)] (well defined, because equivalent states go to equivalent states); start = [s₀]; finals = classes contained in F. If [∅] holds only ∅, it can be left out of the drawing.

MinimizeByPartitions(D): // Moore; Hopcroft is the optimized version
 Π ← { F, S − F }
 repeat
 for each group G of Π:
 split G: p and q stay together if, for every c,
 δ(p,c) and δ(q,c) fall into the SAME group of Π
 until Π doesn't change
Alternative: refining partitions (the Dragon Book's path, Alg. 3.39)
Partitions in the book's DFA ((a|b)*abb)
On 'b', q3 goes to {q4} and the others stay in the big group: Π₁ = { {q0,q1,q2}, {q3}, {q4} }
On 'b', q1 goes to {q3} and q0, q2 go to the big group: Π₂ = { {q0,q2}, {q1}, {q3}, {q4} }
q0 and q2 have identical destinations: Π doesn't change anymore. The same result as the table: q0 ≡ q2.

**Theorem (Myhill–Nerode)**: for each regular language there's a DFA with the minimum number of states, and it is **unique up to renaming the states**. That's why two students who minimize correctly arrive at the same automaton, just with different names.
Which statement is FALSE?
The minimal DFA is unique up to names
The table and the partitions give the same minimal DFA
A pair left unmarked in a round can never be marked again
Unreachable states must be removed first
False: in the book's DFA, {q0,q1} stays blank in round 2 and is marked in round 3. Only at the END (when a whole round marks nothing) does the blank become a verdict of equivalence.

**Cost**: the table has n(n − 1)/2 cells and each round sweeps all of them: polynomial, great for exams with up to ~8 states. Hopcroft's algorithm does the same in O(n · |Σ| · log n) and it's what scanner generators use.

Exam outline: (1) unreachable states out; (2) complete with ∅; (3) staircase table with the ROUND in each cell; (4) repeat until it stabilizes; (5) list the classes; (6) draw the minimal DFA with start and finals. Forgetting step 6 is losing half the question.
Define distinguishable states and say what round 1 marks.
p and q are distinguishable if there's a w with δ*(p, w) ∈ F and δ*(q, w) ∉ F (or vice versa). Round 1 marks every final × non-final pair, whose witness is ε.
Mark, Propagate, Merge
**MPM: Mark, Propagate, Merge.** MARK final × non-final. PROPAGATE the marks through the arrows, round after round. MERGE whoever was left unmarked. (Think 'MPM = Most People Merge'.)

**Memory palace**: in the Lexical Forest, right after the Subset Factory, is the **Table of Pairs** : a stone staircase. Each step has little cells, one for each pair of states. The guard paints the cells of different pairs red; the ones that stay white become a single house.
**A staircase, not a square.** {p,q} = {q,p} and {p,p} doesn't matter: draw only the bottom triangle. n states → n(n−1)/2 cells. With 5 states: 10 cells.
**Final and non-final are oil and water**: they never mix. That's why round 1 is automatic.
**Dominoes**: 'if the CHILDREN are different, the PARENTS are too'. If p and q, on the same letter, land on a red cell, paint {p,q} red.
In round 2, the pair {q0,q1} goes on 'b' to {q2,q3}, which is blank RIGHT NOW. What do you do?
Mark it, because it'll probably get marked
Leave it blank and come back in the next round
Merge q0 and q1
A domino only falls when pushed by a piece that ALREADY fell. In round 3, {q2,q3} is red and then {q0,q1} falls too.
**The dead state votes too.** The ∅ state doesn't talk, doesn't accept anything, but it DISTINGUISHES: without it, a*b* would become (a|b)*. Before drawing the staircase, ask: 'is any arrow missing?'
The three classic stumbles: (1) **forgetting ∅**; (2) **marking based on a cell that's still blank**; (3) **stopping after just one round**, without checking whether the dominoes keep falling.

The Forest's conveyor: **T**hompson **T**ransforms (regex → NFA), **S**ubsets **S**implify (NFA → DFA), **M**inimization **M**erges the repeated ones (DFA → minimal DFA). And the minimum is **unique**: 'each language has a single minimal birth certificate'.
Recite MPM while the widget runs: mark (round 1), propagate (rounds 2 and 3), merge (q0 with q2).
Without looking: the 3 steps and the 3 stumbles.

Steps: Mark final × non-final; Propagate through the arrows until it stabilizes; Merge the blank pairs. Stumbles: forgetting the dead state, marking based on a pair not yet marked, and not repeating the rounds.
Contrast: what does the subset construction do and what does minimization do?
Subsets remove the NONDETERMINISM (NFA → DFA), possibly creating leftover states. Minimization removes the REDUNDANCY (DFA → the smallest equivalent DFA). One doesn't replace the other.
The summary and the whole book
The night before a literature exam. Byte has two options: reread the whole book, with the preface, contents and footnotes, or read a classmate's two-page summary.
The summary, obviously! But... doesn't it lose anything important?

A GOOD summary loses nothing that matters for the exam: characters, who did what, in what order. It only throws away what was there for the book to be READ: transition chapters, page numbers, notes. The **abstract syntax tree (AST)** is the summary; the **parse tree** is the whole book.
Book × summary → parse tree × AST
The whole book → **parse tree (concrete)**: a node for EACH step of the grammar.
Transition chapters ('E becomes T, which becomes F...') → **chain nonterminals**: E → T → F → a. They vanish in the AST.
Page numbers and contents → **parentheses and punctuation**: they were only there for the parser to know the order. The AST's shape already keeps that order.
Blank pages → **ε** productions: they vanish.
Characters and actions → **operators and operands**: they become `BinOp`, `Var`, `Num` nodes.
For 'a + b * c', the parse tree of the E/T/F grammar has 13 nodes. How many does the AST have?
Only the 3 operands and the 2 operators are left: BinOp('+') with Var(a) and BinOp('*') with Var(b) and Var(c). 13 → 5: a real summary!
Side by side: the book (derivation) and the summary (AST). Notice that * is still DEEPER than +: precedence survived.
So the AST is just a skinnier tree. Why is it so important?
Because, after syntax analysis, ALL the rest of the compiler studies from the summary: the type checker, the symbol table, the code generator. Nobody wants to reread the whole book three times.

In the course project (the compiler in Java), many groups translate directly inside the parser: read a token, emit assembly right away. It works, but it's like taking the exam reading the book only once, with no going back. With the AST you read once, build the summary and then can go over it as many times as you want: once to check types, another to generate code.

Q: If I throw away the parentheses, how does the compiler know (a + b) * c is different from a + b * c? A: By the SHAPE of the tree. In (a + b) * c, the + sits under the *; in a + b * c, it's the * that sits under the +. Whatever is deeper is computed first.
In the analogy, who is: the whole book, the summary, a transition chapter, the page numbers?
The parse tree, the AST, a chain nonterminal (E → T → F), parentheses/punctuation.
Tree diet, live
Today each widget shows the same expression twice: the parse tree (fat) and the AST (lean), with the node count and the Java code that builds the AST.

What was left in the AST of '( ( a ) )'?
A BinOp with two children
A single Var(a)
Two parenthesis nodes

Associativity: 14 nodes against 5. See which '-' ended up lower.
In the AST of 'a - b - c', which subtraction is deeper (done first)?
The left one: (a - b) - c
The right one: a - (b - c)
Either way: it gives the same value

The grammar E → E - T is LEFT recursive, so the tree grows to the left: new BinOp('-', new BinOp('-', a, b), c). And it doesn't give the same value: with a=10, b=3, c=2, (10-3)-2 = 5 but 10-(3-2) = 9.
Now with parentheses on the right: 19 nodes against 5. The shape of the AST changed, even without any parenthesis node.

Rules you just saw happen
An id/num leaf → **Var** or **Num** (a single node, without the chain F → id).
A production with an operator (E → E + T) → **BinOp** with the operator and the two children.
A chain production (E → T, T → F) → no new node: it just passes the child along.
In binary expressions: AST nodes = 2 × (number of operators) + 1.
Statements also become nodes (Atrib, Se...). The generator walks this tree and emits the jumps. With a=4 and b=7, it prints 7.
An expression with 10 binary operators: how many nodes does the AST have? And why does the parse tree always have MORE nodes than that?
21 nodes (10 BinOp + 11 leaves). The parse tree has at least one nonterminal node for each AST node, plus the chain nodes, the parenthesis nodes and the operator tokens themselves as leaves.
Building the AST in recursive descent
Remember the recursive descent parser, with one method per nonterminal? The change is small: instead of void, each method **returns an Expr**.
The AST classes (Java, as in the course project)
The parser that BUILDS the AST. The while in expr() and termo() guarantees left associativity.
Tracing '2 * x + y'
fator() sees '2' (a number) → returns **new Num(2)**. In termo(), e = Num(2).
termo() sees '*': matches, calls fator(), which returns **Var(x)**. e = **new BinOp('*', Num(2), Var(x))**.
termo() sees '+', which is neither * nor /: it leaves the while and returns the BinOp('*').
Back in expr(): e = BinOp('*'). It sees '+': matches, calls termo(), which returns **Var(y)**.
e = **new BinOp('+', BinOp('*', Num(2), Var(x)), Var(y))**. End of input: it returns e.
Check it: 13 nodes in the derivation, 5 in the AST, and the generated Java code.

The most important line is `e = new BinOp(op, e, termo());`: the PREVIOUS result becomes the LEFT child of the new node. That's how 'a - b - c' becomes (a - b) - c. If you write recursion (`e = new BinOp(op, e, expr())`), the tree hangs to the right and the subtraction comes out wrong.
Now it's up to you (faded example): **a - ( b - c )**.
What does fator() return when it finds '('?
It matches '(', calls expr(), which builds new BinOp('-', Var(b), Var(c)), matches ')' and returns THAT BinOp. No parenthesis node is created.

In a priority field on each node
In the shape of the tree: the + is a CHILD of the *

It gets lost

And the T node in the middle of the chain E → T → F? Doesn't it do anything?

In the derivation, it records that the grammar went through the * precedence level. But, since there was no *, there's no operation to represent. In the AST, it simply vanishes: the termo() method returns whatever fator() returned.

You've already emitted code for x before knowing the declaration; you'd have to go back

Mention two other advantages of building the AST before generating code.

1) Separation of concerns: the parser only recognizes and builds; the semantics and the generator live in methods of the classes (avaliar, verificarTipo, gerar), which are easier to test. 2) Optimizations like constant folding become 'swap a BinOp(Num, Num) for a Num' on the tree. Bonus: you can print the AST and debug.
And statements, like if and while? What do they become in the AST?
They vanish, like the parentheses
Nodes of their own, like Se(cond, entao, senao) and Enquanto(cond, corpo)
Var leaves
Each construct with meaning becomes a class. Keywords, braces and semicolons vanish; the condition and the body stay as children.
An Enquanto (while) with a Bloco of two Atrib inside. The generator walks the tree and produces the loop with jumps. It prints 6.

Parse tree: 'I have EVERYTHING, every detail!' AST: 'And that's why nobody can stand walking through you three times.' Parse tree: 'Hmph. At least the parser loves me.' AST: 'The parser uses you and hands me over to the rest of the compiler.'
AST: exam definition

**Parse tree (concrete)**: root = start symbol; each internal node is a nonterminal A whose children are the right side of a production A → α used; the leaves, read from left to right, form the sentence.

**Abstract syntax tree (AST)**: each internal node is an **operator or construct** of the language and its children are the meaningful **operands/components**. It omits chain nonterminals (A → B), parentheses, punctuation and ε. The AST isn't unique to the grammar: it's a design choice of the compiler.
Statements as classes (along with Expr, Num, Var, BinOp)

**Syntax-directed construction**: each production gets a semantic rule that synthesizes the attribute `nodo` (the left side's AST) from the children's `nodo`. It's an **S-attributed** definition: the attributes go up from the leaf to the root.
In Bison (bottom-up): $$ is the left side's value; $1, $2, $3 those of the right side's symbols
Because the parenthesis is the 2nd symbol
Because exp is the 2nd symbol on the right side, and the factor's AST is simply exp's AST
To create a parenthesis node
'(' is $1, exp is $2, ')' is $3. Passing $2 along is exactly 'throwing away the parenthesis'.

**Recursive descent**: each nonterminal method returns the AST of what it recognized. For A → A op B (left recursive, removed as A → B (op B)*), use a **loop** that accumulates: `e = new BinOp(op, e, B())`, preserving left associativity.
Walking the AST: each phase is a method (or a Visitor). Notice the post-order: children before the parent.

With many phases, instead of putting avaliar/gerar/verificarTipo in each class, the **Visitor** pattern is used: one class per phase (VerificadorDeTipos, GeradorMips) with a visit method per node type. javac, Roslyn (C#) and Clang are organized around the AST like this.

Three questions that show up: (1) draw the AST of an expression (remember: no parentheses, left associative); (2) write the $$ = new ... actions of a Bison grammar; (3) 'tell the parse tree apart from the AST': answer with the definition + an example with a node count.
Define AST and mention three things it throws away compared with the parse tree.

A tree where internal nodes are operators/constructs and children are meaningful operands. It throws away: chain nonterminals (E → T → F), parentheses/punctuation and ε productions (and, with them, the keywords that only marked the construct).
The tree on a diet
**AST = A Slimmed Tree.** It removes three kinds of clutter: **C**hains (E → T → F), **P**arentheses (and punctuation) and **E**psilons. 'Cut the CPE.'

**Memory palace**: in Semantic City, next to the symbol table's registry office, is the **AST Factory** , a carpentry shop. A huge log arrives (the parse tree); the carpenter saws off the branches that only pass things along, throws away the sawdust of the parentheses and hands over a 5-piece table, ready to use.
**Parentheses are scaffolding**: needed while the building is under construction (parsing), removed when it's done. The building's shape (the tree) already keeps what they were holding.
**A chain message**: E → T → F → a is like a message forwarded five times. The content is the 'a'; the forwards add nothing. In the AST: Var(a), and that's it.
**Whoever is deeper works first.** In the AST of a + b * c, the * is in the basement: it's done first. Depth = precedence.
Which line of code is the 'secret' of left associativity in the top-down parser?
'The old one goes to the left': the accumulated result becomes the new node's left child, on each turn of the loop.
**Bison in three words: 'child becomes parent'.** $$ = new BinOp('+', $1, $3): the children $1 and $3 become children of the new node $$. A chain? $$ = $1. A parenthesis? $$ = $2.

Contrasts that confuse: the **parse tree** has nonterminals and every token; the **AST** has only operators and operands. The **AST** is a structure; **TAC** is a list of instructions generated from it. **Parse tree** = derivation tree = concrete syntax tree (three names, one thing).
Cut the CPE: count the chains and the parentheses and watch 18 become 5.
Without looking: what's thrown away, what stays and where does the precedence live?
Out: chains, parentheses/punctuation, ε. Stays: operators (BinOp) and operands (Var, Num), and constructs (Atrib, Se, Enquanto, Bloco). Precedence and associativity live in the SHAPE of the tree.
Why is it worth building the AST in the project instead of generating code directly in the parser?

Because then the compiler can walk the program several times (types, then code), with each phase separate and testable, and optimize by changing the tree. Direct translation is a single pass, with no going back.
