Few counters in the kitchen
A restaurant kitchen on a wedding day. The pantry in the basement keeps everything, but each trip down the stairs takes forever. Upstairs there are only three counters.
It's the kitchen from the MIPS lesson! A counter is a register, the pantry is memory.

Right. And the new chef does something silly: finishes the sauce, TAKES it to the pantry, and five minutes later goes down again to FETCH the same sauce. That's the naive code: an `sw` followed by an `lw` of the same temporary.
The experienced chef thinks differently: 'The sauce will be used soon, it stays on a counter. When the sauce is used for the last time, the counter becomes FREE for another prep.'
Each intermediate prep (sauce, dough) is a **temporary** (t1, t2, ...).
Each counter is a **register**. There are only k counters.
From the moment the prep is ready until its LAST use, it's **alive** and takes up a counter: that's its **live range**.
Two preps alive AT THE SAME TIME can't share a counter: they **interfere**.
Giving each prep a counter, with no neighbors fighting, is **coloring a graph**: each color is a register.
If there aren't enough counters, some prep goes down to the pantry and is fetched again when needed: that's the **spill**.

It's the same problem as coloring a map of the world: countries that share a border can't have the same color. In allocation, the 'border' is being alive at the same time. Four colors are enough for any flat map, but a program's graph isn't a map: sometimes it needs more.
In r = a * b + c * d: t1 = a * b is ready; then t2 = c * d; then t3 = t1 + t2. Which temporaries need different counters?
t1 and t2
t1 and t3
t2 and t3
All three
When t2 is ready, t1 is still waiting to be used: both are alive together. But t3 is born exactly when t1 and t2 die (they're used for the last time), so t3 can reuse the counter of either one.
See the live ones, the graph (just one edge: t1—t2) and the coloring with 2 registers.
How many trips to the pantry (lw + sw) does the naive code make in this computation, and how many after allocation?
Naive: 11 (7 lw + 4 sw). With 2 registers: 5 (4 lw of the variables a, b, c, d + 1 sw of the result r). Less than half!

Q: Why not just use a different register for each temporary? A: Because a real program has thousands of temporaries and MIPS has 32 registers (and several are reserved). Reusing counters is mandatory.
In the analogy, who is: the counter, the prep, preps that fight, going down to the pantry?
A register, a temporary, temporaries that interfere (alive at the same time, an edge in the graph), a spill to memory.

How the table was filled in
Start at the END: after the last instruction, nothing is alive (out = { }). The variables a..d and r stay in memory, so we only count temporaries.
i=4 (t5 = t1 + t4): out = {t5}; remove the def t5 and add the uses t1, t4 → in = {t1, t4}.
i=3 (t4 = t2 + t3): out = {t1, t4}; remove t4, add t2, t3 → in = {t1, t2, t3}.
i=2 (t3 = a * c): out = {t1, t2, t3}; remove t3 → in = {t1, t2}. Here there are 3 alive together: the peak.
Edges: at each instruction, the DEFINED temporary connects to all the others in out. That gives t2—t1, t3—t1, t3—t2, t4—t1.
Chaitin with k = 3 (simplify, push, color)
Degrees: t1 = 3, t2 = 2, t3 = 2, t4 = 1, t5 = 0. Only remove whoever has degree < 3.
Remove t2 (degree 2) → push. Now t1 has degree 2: remove t1. Then t3, t4, t5 (degree 0).
Stack (top first): t5, t4, t3, t1, t2.
Pop and give the lowest free color: t5 → 0, t4 → 0, t3 → 0, t1 → 1 (neighbors t3, t4 have 0), t2 → 2 (neighbors t1 = 1, t3 = 0).

Classic mistake: doing liveness from TOP to BOTTOM. It doesn't work: to know whether t1 is alive now, you need to know whether it will be used LATER. The information comes from the future, so the analysis moves backward.

Why does the compiler work hard to keep values in registers?
Because memory can erase data
Because accessing memory (lw/sw) is much slower than using a register
Because MIPS forbids lw
To save space in .data
An operation between registers takes one cycle; a trip to memory can cost tens or hundreds of cycles if the data isn't in the cache. Cutting lw/sw is cutting time.
But registers are few. So two values will have to share one?
When can two temporaries x and y use the SAME register?
When they have similar names
When they're never alive at the same time
When they're used in the same instruction
If y only comes into existence after the last use of x, x doesn't need the register anymore. That's the whole idea.
What does 'x is alive at point P' mean?
x was already defined before P
There's a path from P to a USE of x that doesn't go through a new definition of x
x is in a register
x will be printed
Alive = 'the current value will still be read'. If x will be redefined before being read, the current value is dead: it can be discarded.
From that definition comes the formula in = use ∪ (out − def). Explain each piece.
Before the instruction, what's alive is what it USES (use) and what was alive after it (out), minus what it redefines itself (def), because that old value would never be read.
If the formula computes 'in' from 'out', in which direction do we go through the code?
From top to bottom
From bottom to top
To compute the in of instruction i, I need the out, which is the in of i + 1. So I start at the end, with out = { }.
Now build a graph: one node per temporary and an edge between whoever is alive together. Assigning registers is assigning colors without neighbors repeating.
Two colors are enough. Notice which temporary ended up with no neighbors.
And if the graph needs more colors than there are registers?
Some temporary is spilled: it lives in memory, with an sw after it's computed and an lw before each use. Preferably, pick one with many neighbors and few uses.
Why do $t and $s exist separately in MIPS?
Allocation by coloring: exam definition

For each instruction i: **use[i]** = variables read by i; **def[i]** = variables written by i. A variable x is **alive** at a point P if there's a path from P to a use of x that doesn't go through a definition of x.

Liveness (BACKWARD data-flow analysis):
 out[i] = ∪ in[s] for each successor s of i (at the end: out = ∅)
 in[i] = use[i] ∪ (out[i] − def[i])
In a basic block (no jumps), the only successor of i is i + 1:

Liveness equations

**Live range** of x: the program points at which x is alive. **Interference graph** G = (V, E): V = temporaries; {x, y} ∈ E if x is defined at an instruction where y ∈ out (y ≠ x). (Classic refinement: in a copy x = y, x isn't connected to y, so they can share the register.)
**Allocation with k registers** = **k-coloring** of G. Deciding whether G is k-colorable is NP-complete for k ≥ 3, which is why we use heuristics.

Chaitin(G, k):
 stack ← empty
 while G isn't empty:
 if there's an n with degree(n) < k: // SIMPLIFY
 remove n from G; push n
 else: // SPILL candidate
 pick n (e.g. highest degree, lowest cost); remove; push
 while the stack isn't empty: // SELECT
 n ← pop
 if there's a color not used by the already colored neighbors: give the lowest
 else: n is SPILLED (sw after def, lw before each use)
Simplify, push, color

**Why it works**: if degree(n) < k, then, however bad the neighbors' coloring is, a color is left for n. Removing n doesn't get in the way; we color it on the way back. A spill only happens when every remaining node has degree ≥ k.
A graph has a node n with degree 5 and k = 4. What's TRUE?
n will certainly be spilled
n can't be simplified now, but it may end up colored if two neighbors get the same color
The graph isn't 4-colorable
Degree ≥ k only makes n a CANDIDATE. In selection, if the neighbors repeat colors, a color is left for n. That's why Chaitin's spill is 'optimistic' in Briggs's version.

Now the same factorial in MIPS, the way MARS runs it. Each call's frame has 2 words (8 bytes): the `$ra` and the `n`.
**Caller:** puts the argument in `$a0` and runs `jal fat` (which stores the return address in `$ra`)
**Callee, on the way out (epilogue):** puts the result in `$v0`, restores `$ra`, `addi $sp, $sp, 8` closes the frame and `jr $ra` returns
**Caller, afterward:** uses the value that arrived in `$v0`

Forgot to save `$ra` before the inner `jal`? The recursive call overwrites `$ra`, and the final `jr $ra` returns to the wrong place: the program loops. A function that calls another ALWAYS saves `$ra` on the stack.
It stored the **return address** at the moment of the call. In MIPS, `jal` puts that address in `$ra`; since the next call would overwrite `$ra`, it's saved in the frame.

The result goes to an agreed-upon place (in MIPS, `$v0`). To find the previous frame again, the **control link** (dynamic link) is kept, a pointer to the caller's frame; or, in simple MIPS, it's enough to undo `$sp`.
**Caller:** evaluates the actual parameters and puts them where the callee expects them (in the frame, or in `$a0`–`$a3`)
**Callee (prologue):** allocates the frame (`$sp` -= size), saves registers (including `$ra`) and initializes the locals
**Callee (return):** puts the return value in the agreed-upon place (`$v0`), restores registers and `$sp`, jumps to the return address (`jr $ra`)
**jal = Jump And Link**: jumps and leaves a note to come back in `$ra` (**r**eturn **a**ddress). **jr $ra = Jump Register**: goes back following the note.

**MIPS convention**: $t0–$t9 are **caller-saved**: a function can overwrite them at will. $s0–$s7 are **callee-saved**: whoever uses them saves them on the stack and restores them before `jr $ra`. Rule of thumb: a value that crosses a call → $s; a short-lived value → $t.

The strategy for expressions: the registers `$t0…$t9` work like a **stack**. Each expression method takes the next free register, leaves the result in it and returns WHICH one it is. A binary operation does `esq = esq op dir` and gives `dir` back to the pool: it's always the newest one.
